chapters.before_md:
This is a treatise on the oneness of God — tawhid (تَوْحِيد) — and the first volume of a longer work. It does not argue by dry definition; it moves, chapter by chapter, as a road the soul is meant to walk: from a sealed lamp and the journey home toward a God whom no pointing can reach and no name can enclose.

Its central claim is that the oneness of God is not a number but a purity. To speak of Him at all, the book holds, one must strip away every attribute that would liken Him to a created thing — for to name the unnameable is itself a kind of transgression. From there it turns to what oneness actually means, and to the ranks by which a person climbs toward it: the breaking of the self at the nearest rank, and the recognition that every teacher is a threshold to be crossed, not a god to be worshipped in place of God.

The later chapters treat of creation out of nothing and of a justice in which all stand equal, closing with the first who declared that there is no god but He.

No author is named within the volume itself. It speaks throughout not in one man's voice but as a transmitted report, handing down what it teaches rather than claiming it as its own.

chapters.chapter_key: the sealed lamp and the road home
chapters.before_md:
أَعُوذُ بِاللَّهِ مِنَ الشَّيْطَانِ الرَّجِيمِ، بِسْمِ اللَّهِ الرَّحْمَٰنِ الرَّحِيمِ، وَصَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَىٰ رَسُولِهِ وَآلِهِ الطَّيِّبِينَ الطَّاهِرِينَ وَسَلَّمَ عَلَيْهِمْ أَجْمَعِينَ

> "I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. And may Allah's blessings be upon His Messenger and his pure and purified family, and may peace be upon them all."

So the book begins. Its opening section announces what the entire enterprise is for. It begins:

> نَقُولُ: وَلَمَّا كَانَ مَا هُوَ المَقْصُودُ، وَالكَلَامُ عَلَى المَوَدَّةِ الشَّرِيفَةِ المُؤَدِّيَةِ إِلَى الوَاجِبَاتِ الشَّرِيفَةِ حَقِيقَةً مَحْضَةً
>
> "We say: and since that which is intended — and the discourse here — concerns the noble affections that lead to the noble obligations, taken as a pure reality,"

> لَا تَأْوِيلَ فِيهَا وَلَا رَمْزَ مِنْهَا
>
> "in which there is no interpretation and no symbol."

The aim is declared at the door. It is to treat of the noble affections — the *mawaddah* — that carry the soul toward the noble obligations, and to treat of them as a pure reality, *haqiqatan mahdatan*. That phrase carries weight. The book does not set out to explain the *zahir* (الظَّاهِر), the outer exoteric sense, nor does it climb into *taweel*, the esoteric interpretation. It sets out to lay the pure, unmixed reality of these matters plainly out.

The denial itself is phrased with force, and the grammar sharpens the claim. The words لَا تَأْوِيلَ are read with what the grammarians call *nafi al-jins*, the negation of the genus, an absolute and categorical denial. Had the text said merely لَا تَأْوِيلٌ فِيهِ, it would mean only that some particular interpretation is absent. But لَا تَأْوِيلَ means that there is no interpretation whatsoever — none of the kind, not a trace of the genus. The same holds for what follows: وَلَا رَمْزَ مِنْهَا — and no symbol, no *ramz* (رَمْز), from it, and no *ishara* (إِشَارَة), no allusion either. The intention, then, is pure reality, stripped alike of veiling interpretation, of symbol, and of allusion. That is the declared method, and the book does no more.

From there the discourse opens outward to take in everything that exists. The text goes on:

> ثُمَّ الكَلَامُ عَلَى كَافَّةِ المَوْجُودَاتِ
>
> "Then the discourse is upon all existing things."

The book proposes to take as its subject all the existents that appeared before our own existence. And it states at once why it must:

> إِذْ بِمَعْرِفَةِ ذَٰلِكَ وَالِاطِّلَاعِ عَلَيْهِ، وَطَاعَةِ أَوْلِيَاءِ اللَّهِ وَمَحَبَّتِهِمْ، وَالتَّقَرُّبِ إِلَى اللَّهِ بِهِمْ، وَبِلُزُومِ حُدُودِهِمُ المَنْسُوبِينَ مِنْ قِبَلِ القَائِمِ، بِالعِلْمِ وَالعَمَلِ بِمَا وَرَدَ مِنَ الشَّرَائِعِ، يُهْتَدَىٰ إِلَىٰ تَوْحِيدِ اللَّهِ تَعَالَىٰ وَتَكَبَّرَ
>
> "For by the gnosis of that, and the acquaintance with it, and obedience to the Friends of Allah and love for them, and drawing near to Allah through them, and adhering to their appointed Hudud from the direction of the Qaim — with the knowledge and the action that have come through the religious laws — one is guided to the Oneness of Allah, the Exalted and the Supreme."

It is through the *marifah* (الْمَعْرِفَة) — the gnosis — of all those existing things that came into being before us, through truly knowing them and gaining acquaintance with them, that the soul is first set on the road. It is through obedience to the *Awliya Allah*, the Friends of Allah, and through love of them, and through drawing near to Allah by their means, that the road is actually traveled. Bound up with this is adherence to their حُدُود, the ranks and bounds appointed for the believer, for these حُدُود are *mansubin*, appointed and assigned, from the direction of the Qaim himself, the way a sealed letter is handed down through ordained bearers, each in his place, before it can reach the one for whom it was written. And it is through the action, the عَمَل, laid down in the *shariah* (شَرِيعَة), the religious law, that the road is at last completed. By the whole of this together — gnosis, obedience, love, nearness, adherence to the appointed حُدُود, and lawful action — one is guided toward the تَوْحِيد of Allah, the Most High. This is the only road by which the تَوْحِيد of Allah is reached.

Two pillars carry the whole access. Access to the تَوْحِيد of Allah is attained through two things, and through two things only: وِلَايَة and عَمَل — allegiance and action. *Wilayah* is named here also as *muwalat*, loyal allegiance, and as *muhabbah*, love; it is the bond of devotion to the Friends of Allah. And عَمَل is the deed, the action the law lays down. By these two together — by loving allegiance and by righteous action — access is gained. There is no third way through. And the fruit of that attainment is itself twofold, as the text declares:

> وَبِذَٰلِكَ تَعْلُو دَرَجَةُ المَعَادِ
>
> "And by that, the ranks of the afterlife are elevated,"

> وَيَكُونُ الخَلَاصُ مِنْ هَٰذَا العَالَمِ الكَوْنِ وَالفَسَادِ
>
> "and salvation comes from this world of being and corruption."

By treading this path the ranks of the *maad*, the afterlife, are raised up for the soul, and salvation is won from this lower world of being and corruption — this realm of generation and decay in which, for now, we are held.

That salvation, understood at its deepest, is a homecoming. The text continues:

> وَيُمْكِنُ القَوْدُ إِلَى المَبْدَإِ الَّذِي مِنْهُ الِابْتِدَاءَاتُ الشَّرِيفَةُ
>
> "And it becomes possible to return to the origin from which the noble beginnings came,"

> وَالكَوْنُ مَعَهُمْ فِي دَارِ القُدْسِ
>
> "and to dwell with them in the Abode of Sanctity."

Here the doctrine of return is laid open. *Qawd* is the leading-back, the return, toward the *mabda*, the origin — back to that source from which the noble beginnings, the *ibtidaat*, first issued, the way a river finds its channel before it can ever reach the field it was meant to water. The soul does not belong to this lower world; this is not its native country. Our original homeland — our *watan-e-asli* — is the world of spirits, the عَالَمُ اَلرُّوح. That is the land we came from, and the whole movement of the religious life is nothing but a turning back toward it. The goal is to make our way home to that origin, and there — وَالكَوْنُ مَعَهُمْ فِي دَارِ القُدْسِ — to dwell together with the Friends of Allah in *dar al-quds*, the Abode of Sanctity. As the text prays:

> بَلَّغَنَا اللَّهُ إِلَيْهِمْ، وَأَعَانَنَا عَلَى الِارْتِقَاءِ وَالوُصُولِ إِلَيْهِمْ، بِحَقِّ مُحَمَّدٍ وَآلِهِ الطَّاهِرِينَ، صَلَوَاتُ اللَّهِ عَلَيْهِمْ أَجْمَعِينَ
>
> "May Allah cause us to reach them, and aid us in the ascent and the arrival to them — by the right of Muhammad and his pure progeny, the blessings of Allah be upon them all."

The text then names this knowledge of the origin with an image:

> وَهَٰذَا هُوَ العِلْمُ الَّذِي يَدُورُونَ عَلَيْهِ وَيَجُورُونَ لَدَيْهِ
>
> "And this is the knowledge around which they revolve, and toward which they incline."

This is the knowledge every creature circles. Each person, each created thing, longs to move toward it and to take hold of it; it is the knowledge of the *asl*, the root — the knowledge of the *mabda*, the origin — the answer to the oldest question we carry: where did we come from, what was our beginning. All the creatures, the *khalaiq*, are wheeling around this knowledge, making their endless rounds about it, aching to know where their origin lies. And yet, for all that circling, they cannot reach it:

> وَلَا سَبِيلَ لِأَحَدٍ مِنْهُمْ إِلَيْهِ
>
> "And there is no path for any of them to it."

For the generality of creatures there is no path at all to this knowledge. They revolve forever about a center they will never touch.

There is, however, one exception, and it decides everything:

> إِلَّا القَلِيلَ
>
> "Except for a few —"

> مِمَّنِ اعْتَصَمَ بِالأَئِمَّةِ مِنْ آلِ مُحَمَّدٍ، سَلَامُ اللَّهِ عَلَيْهِمْ أَجْمَعِينَ، وَالْتَزَمَ حُدُودَهُمُ المَيَامِنَ
>
> "from among those who held fast to the Imams from the progeny of Muhammad, the peace of Allah be upon them all, and bound themselves to their blessed Hudud."

The few who reach the knowledge of the origin are precisely those who held fast to the *aimma* (أَئِمَّة), the Imams from the household of Muhammad, and who bound themselves to the true and blessed حُدُود of those Imams. Only these reach the far side. Only these break out of the circle. The rest go on revolving, lifetime after lifetime, around a goal they cannot attain. And so the matter stands plainly: the knowledge of the origin is not yielded to bare seeking, however fierce the seeking grows. It is granted only to the hand that holds fast to the Imams and submits to their appointed ranks.

chapters.chapter_key: the god no pointing can reach
chapters.before_md:
A question has run beneath all of this without being named. What came before treated the seeking, the circle, and the far side reached only by those who bind themselves to the Imams. But the object of that seeking, the One toward whom every step is directed, has not yet been examined. Here the matter turns from the seeker to Him.

The text opens:

> وَكَانَ لَا دَلِيلَ عَلَىٰ ذِكْرِ ذَٰلِكَ إِلَّا بِذِكْرِ اللَّهِ تَعَالَىٰ وَتَكَبَّرَ، الَّذِي بِذِكْرِهِ فِي كُلِّ شَيْءٍ يُسْتَفْتَحُ، وَبِأَسْمَائِهِ الْحُسْنَىٰ يُتَوَسَّلُ إِلَيْهِ فِي كُلِّ مَطْلُوبٍ وَيُسْتَنْجَحُ
>
> "And there was no guide to the mention of that except by the mention of Allah, the Exalted and Supreme — by whose mention every thing is opened, and by whose most beautiful names a means is sought to Him in every request, and success is attained."

There is no path to the mention of these realities except by first mentioning Allah. Without His mention, nothing opens. The word *opened* — `yustaftahu` — comes from *fataha*, to open, yet it has taken the *istifal* shape, the shape of seeking. *Istiftah*, also called *iftitah*, does not merely mean to open; it means to seek the opening, to make the request that a thing be begun at all. So the verse says that by the mention of Allah every thing is not merely unlocked — its very unlocking is asked for and granted. Then `wa bi-asmaihi al-husna` — by His most beautiful names, the *asma al-husna* (الْأَسْمَاءُ الْحُسْنَى) — `yutawassalu ilayhi`, a means is taken to Him. That word too has a root: *wasala*, to connect, to arrive. A *tawassul* is the cord thrown to bridge a distance. Through His names, `fi kulli matlubin` — in every object of seeking, every *matlub*, the thing sought, as against the *talib*, the one who does the seeking — `yustanjahu`, success is granted, from *najaha*. Through His names, in every request, the request lands.

The text now lays down the cornerstone, the stone on which the whole house of belief rests:

> وَكَانَ مُسَبَّحًا مُتَعَالِيًا عَنْ أَنْ يَقَعَ عَلَيْهِ إِشَارَةُ مُشِيرٍ، أَوْ يَتَجَاسَرَ نَحْوَهُ خَاطِرُ خَاطِرٍ بِتَوَهُّمٍ أَوْ تَفْكِيرٍ
>
> "And He is the One glorified, exalted far above that any indicator's indication should fall upon Him, or that the thought of any thinker should dare toward Him by imagination or by contemplation."

He is *musabbah* — the One whose glorification is performed — in the form *musabbah*, not *musabbih*, the glorifier. Human beings are the glorifiers; the *tasbih* (تَسْبِيح) is theirs to offer, never His to perform. He is *mutaali*, the One lifted on high, from the root *uluww*, height. He is lifted so high that no *ishara* (إِشَارَة) — no pointing of any pointer — can fall upon Him so as to indicate Him. This is the true statement of the matter, the very foundation on which correct doctrine stands: no indication reaches Him. And no thought can cross over to Him either. The verb *yatajasaru* comes from *jisr*, a bridge. The *khatir*, the passing thought of the heart, tries to throw a bridge toward Him and cannot complete the span — not by *tawahhum*, imagination, and not by *tafkir*, reasoning. No imagining arrives; no argument arrives. Human beings can know this much and only this much: that since they were made, there is One who made them. But what He is in Himself, what His nature is — of this they know nothing whatever.

This truth lives in a single exchange. In the days of the Commander of the Faithful, a man named Ibn al-Kawwa came to him, meaning to trap him with a question he was sure could not be answered. He asked:

> هَلْ رَأَيْتَ رَبَّكَ؟
>
> "Have you seen your God? Have you seen Allah?"

And Imam Ali answered him:

> وَيْلَكَ، أَفَأَعْبُدُ رَبًّا لَمْ أَرَهُ؟
>
> "Woe to you — could I worship a God I had not seen? How could I worship a God without having seen Him?"

The man pressed him further: how, then, had he seen Him? And the Mawla replied:

> لَمْ تَرَهُ الْعُيُونُ بِمُشَاهَدَةِ الْعِيَانِ، وَلَٰكِنْ رَأَتْهُ الْقُلُوبُ بِحَقَائِقِ الْإِيمَانِ
>
> "The eyes did not see Him by the witnessing of sight; rather the hearts saw Him by the realities of faith."

The meaning is that he saw Him not with the eyes but with the *basirah*, with insight. It is a mighty saying. The vision of Allah is not the vision of the physical eye, which can no more fall upon Him than indication or thought can. It is the vision of insight, the inner perception of the heart that affirms Him without ever closing a hand around His essence.

From this height, something hard and exact follows about His names and His attributes. The text:

> وَكَانَ الْإِعْرَابُ عَنْهُ بِاللَّهِ تَعَالَىٰ وَبِالْمُبْدِعِ بِالْهُوِيَّةِ الْمُتَعَالِيَةِ، غَيْرَ وَاقِعٍ عَلَيْهِ هَذَانِ الِاسْمَانِ وَالصِّفَةُ
>
> "And the expression about Him by Allah, the Exalted, and by the Originator, with the exalted Ipseity — these two names and the attribute do not fall upon Him."

When a name is said of Him — when He is called *Allah Taala*, or *Mubdi* (المُبدِع), the Originator, or reached for by the exalted *huwiyyah*, the Ipseity, the bare "He," the naked *huwa* — none of these names lands on Him. No attribute lands on Him. The reason is given with a knife's precision:

> إِذِ الْأَسْمَاءُ وَالصِّفَاتُ لَا تَقَعُ إِلَّا عَلَىٰ مِثْلِهَا
>
> "For names and attributes do not fall except upon their like."

A name reaches only what is of its own kind; an attribute clings only to something like itself. Naming Him works like this. A person, wanting to recognize and know Him, assigns Him a name, and assigns it from his own tongue. But he is the one who made that tongue; he is the one who minted those names. The very instrument by which a person tries to interpret Allah is a thing of his own manufacture. As the Commander of the Faithful said:

> الْأَسْمَاءُ وَالصِّفَاتُ دَلَالَةٌ عَلَى الْمُسَمَّى
>
> "Names and attributes are an indication pointing to the named one."

And they point only to their like. Mercy was seen in some creature, and so the word "Merciful" was lifted and laid upon that creature; the attribute fell upon its like — upon a knowledge and an arrangement, `ala al-ilmi wa al-tadbir`, of exactly the kind the senses could take in.

One step further on the names themselves, and the ground gives way. These names and attributes are *muhdathah* — originated, brought-into-being things. Everything turns on the distinction: *muhdith* is the one who originates; *muhdath* is the thing originated. The names are *muhdath*. They are made; they are not their own makers. And they are made by a very particular maker — by a human being. A human mouth pronounces a name, a human will assigns it. A person names a child; that person is the one who gave the name. These, then, are names given by human beings, *muhdathah*, brought into being by them. The crux follows:

> وَالْمُحْدَثُ لَا يَقَعُ عَلَى الْمُحْدِثِ مِثْلُهُ
>
> "And the originated thing does not fall upon its originator as its like."

A made thing cannot land on its maker as though they were equals. The fashioned cannot characterize the Fashioner as though they shared a single kind. Sayyidna Muayyad al-Din said exactly this — no minor voice; he lived in the time of Mawlana Mustansir Billah and held the rank of *Bab al-Abwab* (بَابُ الْأَبْوَاب), the Gate of Gates:

> وَلَمَّا كَانَتِ الْحُرُوفُ الْمُعْجَمَةُ مُحْدَثَةً، لَمْ تَكُنْ تَدُلُّ عَلَى الْمُبْدِعِ الصَّانِعِ لَهَا دَلَالَةً مُحَقِّقَةً مُصَدِّقَةً عَلَىٰ مِثْلِهَا
>
> "And since the letters of the alphabet are originated things, they could not indicate the originating Maker who made them with a true and verifying indication upon His like."

The letters cannot turn around and truly point at the One who originated the letters.

Here a fair objection rises, and the text does not dodge it. Someone will say: it is a clean argument that human beings make their own words — but they are limited creatures, and many things run on by His command long before any word leaves their mouths; are they really the makers of *these* things? The answer holds to the precise point in dispute. The words a person speaks now — these he does indeed make; of these spoken words, he is the maker. The whole argument rests on the small but real faculty of choice and making that human beings do possess. With their own handiwork — this tongue, these names that are theirs — they are trying to characterize their own Creator. That, and only that, is what cannot be done. The choice they have is genuine; it simply does not reach far enough to recognize Him. Human beings have no power of choice by which to know Him. He dwells in such a *ghayb*, such an unseen, that its curtains cannot so much as be lifted. Only this can be said: to establish that they themselves exist, human beings affirm that there must be an Originator for them. Who He is, what He is — that stays on the other side of the veil.

Then the question becomes unavoidable. If the names and the attributes do not fall on Allah, then upon what *do* they fall? The text answers:

> وَإِذْ كَانَ الْقَوْلُ كَذَٰلِكَ، كَانَتْ هَذِهِ الْأَسْمَاءُ وَالصِّفَاتُ مَنْفِيَّةً عَنِ اللَّهِ تَعَالَىٰ وَتَكَبَّرَ، وَكَانَتْ وَاقِعَةً عَلَىٰ إِبْدَاعِهِ الَّذِي هُوَ الْعَقْلُ الْأَوَّلُ
>
> "And since the matter is thus, these names and attributes are negated from Allah, the Exalted and Supreme, and they fall instead upon His origination, which is the First Intellect."

Every one of these names, every attribute, is *manfiyyah* — negated, lifted off — from Allah Taala. None is predicated of Him at all. They come to rest instead on His *ibda* (إبداع), His origination. And that origination is the *aql al-awwal*, the First Intellect, which carries other names too: the *mawjud al-awwal*, the first existent, and the *sadir al-awwal*, the first thing to issue forth. The image is of a sealed letter passing through several hands before it reaches the one to whom it is addressed: the names and attributes are delivered as far as this first recipient and no further — negated from Allah and descending upon this first origination, this First Intellect that is at once the first to exist and the first to emanate.

The text drives the blade further:

> وَمَا ظَهَرَ مِنْ فِعْلِهِ فِي اخْتِرَاعِهِ، لَا مِنْ جِهَةِ اسْمٍ وَلَا صِفَةٍ يَخْتَرِعَانِ عَلَيْهِ، لِأَنَّ ذَٰلِكَ مَسْلُوبٌ عَنْهُ، وَاقِعٌ عَلَىٰ إِبْدَاعِهِ
>
> "And what appeared from His act in His creation — not from the aspect of any name or attribute that would be applied specifically to Him — for that is stripped from Him, and falls rather upon His origination."

All that can ever be spoken of is what appeared from His act in His creating — never a name or an attribute pinned directly onto Him. Every such predication is *maslub*: stripped off, severed clean away from Him. The names applied fall upon what He created, upon His *ibda*. And here the matter grows subtler still, and the subtlety cuts deep: if these names and attributes do not even rest fully upon His origination, how could they ever rest upon Allah, the *Mubdi* Most High?

The teaching now opens its arms to the whole of creation and gathers all of it into a single incapacity:

> وَالْعَجْزُ شَامِلٌ لِجَمِيعِ عَالَمِ الْعَقْلِ وَعَالَمِ الْحِسِّ
>
> "And inadequacy is comprehensive over the entire world of intellect and the world of sense."

*Ijz* — inadequacy, the sheer inability to know the Originator — is comprehensive. It covers everything, taking in the *alam al-aql*, the world of intellect, and the *alam al-hiss*, the world of the senses, both together. The First Intellect itself — the highest of all created things — shares in this incapacity, and so does the lowest creature. In this one thing all stand level. As the text says:

> يَتَسَاوَىٰ فِي ذَٰلِكَ الْقَادِرُ وَالْمَقْدُورُ وَالْمَحْسُوسُ وَالْمَعْقُولُ مِنَ الْعَالَمَيْنِ جَمِيعًا
>
> "In that, they are equal — the powerful and the overpowered, the sensed and the intelligible, from both worlds together."

The verb is *yatasawa*, from *sawa*, equal, in the form that carries mutual leveling: it declares them all equal to one another in this single respect. The powerful and the powerless, the sensed thing and the thing grasped by intellect, the world of mind and the world of body — every one of them stands on perfectly flat ground before the unknowability of the Originator. No one is closer than another. No rank lifts its bearer one inch nearer to comprehending Him.

What, then, happens when the word "Allah" is said? The text gives an answer of startling depth:

> وَقَوْلُنَا اللَّهُ إِعْرَابٌ بِهَذَا الِاسْمِ لِإِلْهَانِ الْعَقْلِ الْأَوَّلِ
>
> "And our saying Allah is an expression by this name on account of the bewilderment of the First Intellect."

The saying of "Allah" — the reaching for Him through this name — rises out of *ilhan*, bewilderment, *walah*, the stunned standing-still of the First Intellect before the Originator. The Intellect is bewildered before Him, and out of that bewilderment the word "Allah" breaks from it. And in this, once more, everyone is equal. The Imam is equal in it; the ardent lover, the *ashiq*, is equal in it. Whoever stands bewildered before Him reaches for the same word: "Allah."

The image the matter itself reaches for is the circle. Allah is the *markaz*, the center, the single central point; and around that center the bewildered circle turns. The circle turns because it is bewildered about its center. One circle revolves around its center in bewilderment. Then another circle comes, bewildered about its own center, and it too revolves. Every circle turns around its center, and the reason for the turning is always the one same reason: bewilderment. The very energy by which a circle goes round is, in truth, nothing but its perplexity. The whole created order wheels eternally about a center it cannot comprehend, and the motion of that wheeling is the unceasing bewilderment of the creature before the One who made it.

The text now recounts the first act of all — the primal moment in which the First Intellect first denied divinity, then affirmed it:

> وَقَوْلُنَا الْهُوِيَّةُ الْمُتَعَالِيَةُ: لَمَّا نَفَىٰ عَنْهُ وَعَنْ أَبْنَاءِ جِنْسِهِ الْإِلَٰهِيَّةَ، وَأَثْبَتَهَا لَهُ تَعَالَىٰ وَتَكَبَّرَ، كَمَا أَخْبَرَ عَنْهُ الْكِتَابُ الْكَرِيمُ بِقَوْلِهِ: شَهِدَ اللَّهُ أَنَّهُ لَا إِلَٰهَ إِلَّا هُوَ
>
> "And our saying the exalted Ipseity — when he negated from himself and from the members of his genus the divinity, and affirmed it for Him, the Exalted and Supreme, as the Noble Book informed concerning him in His saying: Allah testifies that there is no god but He."

The First Intellect did this. Contemplating the Originator, it first performed a negation, declaring in effect that it was not the maker of itself. It pronounced `la ilaha` — there is no god — and pushed divinity away from itself: it had no power to create itself, nor did its genus, the whole order of beings like it, have any power to create. It stripped *al-ilahiyyah*, divinity, off itself and off its own kind. And then it affirmed that divinity for Allah Taala alone — `illa Hu`, except He.

This is the very pattern the Noble Book has set down:

> شَهِدَ اللَّهُ أَنَّهُ لَا إِلَٰهَ إِلَّا هُوَ
>
> "Allah testifies that there is no god but He."

The deep sense is this: the "Allah" who testifies in this verse is the First Intellect. It is the First Intellect that bears witness `annahu la ilaha illa Hu` — that there is no god but He, the *Mubdi* Most High. The First Intellect, and with it the entire order of created being, first confessed that it could not create itself or its kind, and then pointed past itself with `illa Hu` — He alone — toward the Originator, who can be indicated by nothing more than the bare pronoun "He."

The text closes the thought:

> وَلَيْسَ يَقَعُ عَلَيْهِ شَيْءٌ مِنْ ذَٰلِكَ إِلَّا كَبِيرًا مِنْ قَوْلِهِ هُوَ، وَسَنُبَيِّنُ حَقِيقَةَ ذَٰلِكَ إِنْ شَاءَ اللَّهُ تَعَالَىٰ
>
> "And nothing of that falls upon Him save, perhaps, His saying He — and we shall clarify the reality of that matter, if Allah the Exalted wills."

> فَأَعْرَبَ عَنْهُ بِمَا كَانَ مِنْ صِفَةِ إِبْدَاعِهِ وَفِعْلِهِ
>
> "So he expressed about Him by what belonged to the attributes of His origination and His act."

The Intellect could express Him only through what showed itself in the origination, saying, in effect, that He had created and fashioned it so. The creature cannot praise the Creator as He deserves, not knowing Him. But from the plain fact of its own existence, from the very manner in which He shaped it, the creature can say something true: He gave it life, He gave it knowledge, He gave it power. That much may be said, because that much the creature itself holds and knows. But the true *tamjid*, the real glorification, the highest praise that would actually befit Him — that lies past its reach entirely. The very highest word that can be lifted toward Him is "Allah," and one step above that, "Huwa" — He. Beyond those two words nothing remains in human hands with which to interpret Him.

So the seeking treated earlier, and the holding fast to the Imams, now have their true horizon in view. The whole endeavor has strained toward a center that no eye reaches, no name lands on, no thought bridges — One whom even the First Intellect could only stand bewildered before and confess with a single pronoun. The word "He" has been left standing alone at the end, deliberately, like a door not yet opened. The text has promised to clarify its reality — and that bare "Huwa," that last and highest thing the tongue can say, is exactly where the matter goes next.

chapters.chapter_key: the sin of naming the unnameable
chapters.before_md:
فَوَقَعَ لِنُوقِعَ عَلَى الْهُوِيَّةِ الْمُتَعَالِيَةِ لِعَجْزِنَا وَضِيقِ جَوْهَرِنَا وَحَصْرِنَا وَقُصُورِنَا

> "And so it came about that we should let the name fall upon the exalted Ipseity — because of our inadequacy, the narrowness of our essence, our confinement, and our deficiency."

At the bare "He," a sharp question waits. If no name lands on Him, why name Him at all? Why reach for words already known to miss?

The answer is not flattering, and it is not meant to be. He is named out of poverty. That last word — *He*, the Ipseity, the *huwiyyah* — is let fall upon Him not because it fits, but because there is nothing left. The reasons the text gives stand one beside the next. There is our *ijz*, our sheer inadequacy, the inability of a created thing to hold its Creator in thought. There is the *diq*, the narrowness, of our *jawhar* (الْجَوْهَر) — and *jawhar* here is the very substance of us, the essence out of which our speech and our articulation, our *nutq*, are made. The instrument we would measure Him with is too small for the measuring. Our *hiss*, our faculty of sense, is hemmed in on every side. We are deficient, and we are constrained, and the name laid upon Him is simply the last syllable our minds can reach before the ground gives out. Beyond it there is nothing further to say. The naming is not a triumph of language. It is the sound a confined creature makes at the edge of its confinement.

The precision of this turns on a distinction between what was given and what was not. The created intellects — the high spiritual realities through which everything descends — were given *ilm al-kulli*, total knowledge. That phrase can mislead. Total knowledge does not mean knowledge of God. It means, as Sayyidna Muayyad explains, *ilm al-hayat*, the knowledge of life: a complete grasp of what powers and faculties live inside life itself. He sets them out plainly — *hayat*, life; *ilm*, knowledge; *quwwah*, power; *ikhtiyar* (اَلْاِخْتِيَار), choice — and then expounds each one at length, what life is, what knowledge is, what power is, what choice is. The intellects know all of that, top to bottom, with nothing left over. But the knowledge by which one would know Allah was never handed to them. It was withheld. It was withheld because it cannot even be comprehended — there is no faculty into which it could be poured. The image is of a house whose every room one has walked, whose wiring and beams and foundations one could draw from memory; the structure of the dwelling is known entirely, and still the One who built it has never been met. That is the position of the created intellects. They know the architecture of life in its fullness. The essence of the One who gave the life stays sealed.

There is a companion teaching from Sayyidna Muayyad here, about the permanence of what Allah bestows. Once He has given existence, He does not take it back. A man who gives a thing to another does not afterward snatch it out of his hands; and so too, having granted existence, Allah does not withdraw it. This sounds at first like a gentle observation. It opens, in fact, onto a hard question about divine power — the kind of question raised to corner a believer.

There was once a debate between an Arya Samaji and the Muslims, and the man set his trap carefully. "Your Allah can do everything?" he asked. The Muslims said, "Yes." "Then can He do *zulm*, injustice? If He can do all things, He can do injustice too. And if you say He cannot, then you have just put a limit on His power." It is a clever knot. The Muslims did not argue it; they answered it with a question of their own. "Can you eat everything? You have the power to eat — so eat this filth set before you." The man could not, of course. Possessing the capacity to eat lays no obligation on one to swallow what is vile. Capacity is one thing; the swallowing is another. In just the same way, Allah is capable of all things, and He does not do injustice — and His not doing it takes nothing away from His power. It is not a wall around His ability. It is the perfection of His justice. He can do everything, and He does not do wrong, and He does not reclaim the existence He has given. The two hold together: total capacity, and a will that does no injustice. They do not contradict.

A prayer now exposes a paradox sitting at the root of all this naming. Sayyidna Muayyad — here meaning Hibatullah ibn Musa al-Shirazi, the spiritual son of Mawlana Sayyidna Muayyad al-Din, the author of the *Mabda wa Maad* — says in some of his words:

اللَّهُمَّ يَا مَنْ وَقَعَ اعْتِرَافُنَا بِصِدْقِ مَا قَالَهُ فِي حَكِيمِ ذِكْرِهِ، إِذْ يَقُولُ وَقَوْلُهُ الْحَقُّ: وَمَا قَدَرُوا اللَّهَ حَقَّ قَدْرِهِ

> "O Allah, O You to whom our confession is rendered, attesting the truth of what He said in His wise remembrance, when He says — and His word is the truth — And they have not appraised Allah with His true appraisal."

What is confessed here is the truth of His own verdict on us: that they have not measured the worth of Allah with His true worth. We cannot appraise Him as He deserves, and we never will, because we do not know Him. The most we can say is what we say from inside our own existence — that, judging by the goodness of what we ourselves are, He has made something good. That is the ceiling of our praise. It is a praise of the gift, offered by someone who has never seen the Giver.

And so the prayer turns, in the same breath, to asking pardon:

إِنَّا نَسْأَلُكَ الْمُسَامَحَةَ لِمَنْ هُوَ مِنْ رِبْقِ الْعُبُودِيَّةِ فِي مَضِيقِ الْحِصَارِ وَالتَّضْيِيقِ، إِذَا أَرَدْنَا تَنَاوُلَ ذِكْرِكَ بِغَيْرِ مَا أَنْتَ أَهْلُهُ

> "Indeed we ask You for forbearance toward one who is in the noose of servitude, in the narrow straits of confinement and constraint, when we set ourselves to undertake Your remembrance by that which You are not worthy of."

We are asking for *musamahah* — forbearance, pardon; the word comes from *samaha*, to forgive. And for whom is it asked? For the one caught in the *rubq*, the snare, of servitude, of *ubudiyyah*. We are bound servants, drawn tight in the noose of our own creaturehood, hemmed in by the narrow straits of confinement — *hisar* — with limits set around us that we cannot step past. And when we rise to undertake His remembrance, we are forced to do it by means unworthy of Him, because the only means worthy of Him is the one we cannot reach. We say as much as our strength allows. And exactly where our strength fails and the words fall short of Him, there we ask His pardon.

The prayer then gives the reason the pardon is needed, and it gives it without softening:

لِأَنَّ تَنَاوُلَ ذِكْرِكَ بِغَيْرِ مَا أَنْتَ أَهْلُهُ بِحُكْمِ الِاضْطِرَارِ فَإِنَّمَا هُوَ ذَنْبٌ مَشْفُوعٌ بِالِاسْتِغْفَارِ

> "Because to undertake Your remembrance by that which You are not worthy of, under the rule of compulsion, is only a sin coupled with the seeking of forgiveness."

The phrase is built with care. To take up His remembrance with our inadequate words is done *bi-hukmi al-idtirar* — by the rule of compulsion, of necessity. We are compelled. Out of *idtirar* we have no other word to offer, so we offer the only one we have. And therefore the act is *dhanbun mashfuun bi-al-istighfar* — a sin coupled with the seeking of forgiveness. This is a term the دُعَاة established with precision: a *dhanb*, a sin, that is *mashfu* — paired, joined — with *istighfar* (اِسْتِغْفَار), the asking of pardon. The word *mashfu* is from *shafaa*, to make a pair. So this is a sin that never travels alone. It comes already wedded to the plea for forgiveness, and because it arose out of compulsion, it is accepted — for compulsion is excusable. There is no arrogance in it. There is the utmost humility in it, the humility of a creature who speaks of his Lord knowing every word is too small, and asks pardon for the smallness in the very act of speaking.

Care is needed on one further point: this does not apply to the physical world alone. It applies to every world equally. The *istighfar* is required of all — and the First Intellect, the *Mubda al-Awwal* itself, is included with everyone else. The claim is arresting. The First Intellect committed no transgression; there is no moral crime here. So the "sin" cannot be a sin in the ordinary sense. Rather — even the First Intellect's own act carries this character within it. When it says that *You are the Mubdi (المُبدِع), the Originator, Most High*; when it bears its witness —

شَهِدَ اللَّهُ أَنَّهُ لَا إِلَٰهَ إِلَّا هُوَ

> "Allah bears witness that there is no god but He" —

and indicates Him by nothing more than *illa Huwa*, by the bare pronoun *He*, because there is simply nothing beyond that to point with — even this, the highest utterance in all of creation, falls short of His true majesty. And because it falls short, it too is coupled with *istighfar*. From the First Intellect down to the tenth, not one of them can do a hair more than this. All are compelled. All stand equal before the Creator, the Originator, whom none of them can recognize. The rank does not change the position. The first intellect and the tenth are level on this single point: the One above them is unknowable to every one of them.

How compulsion changes the weight of an act appears in a case judged in the time of Umar. A woman was brought before him carrying a child, and she said she had no husband. Asked how this had happened, she told them: she had been crossing the desert, dying of thirst, three days without water, when she came upon a shepherd. He said he would give her water on one condition — that she give herself to him. At the edge of death, for the sake of the water, she yielded; and afterward she bore the child. Umar said, "Stone her." A child, no marriage, no husband. But the Mawla of all creation, Imam Ali, arrived and asked what the matter was, and when he heard it he said: "She is *mustarr* — compelled, helpless. Let her go. This happened under *idtirar*, under compulsion." *Idtirar* is helplessness itself, and where there is true helplessness the act does not carry the full weight of a sin.

So it is with the soul that names the Unnameable. In its helplessness it sins, in a manner of speaking, by speaking inadequately of Him. But because it is compelled, that sin comes paired with the asking of forgiveness, and it is excused. A strange paradox lingers — that even in the pure world of the spirits, where everything is illumined except His essence, there could be any possibility of "sin" at all. The paradox is resolved exactly in the coupling. Nothing more than this can be done. It is compulsion. And so neither the first intellect nor the tenth can do otherwise; and in the matter of the Creator, the Originator, every one of them is equal, because not one of them can recognize Him.

The ladder itself now stands out — the *maratib*, the ascending ranks of spirituality through which the soul mounts toward its origin. The way the channel of a river is cut before any water can run through it, these ranks are the channel of the ascent. The lowest of those named is the Imamate of spirituality, the rank of *Rutbat al-Ilahiyyah* in its rising order; and from there the stations climb in sequence — حُجِّيَّة, then حِجَابِيَّة, then خَيَالِيَّة, then فَتْحِيَّة, then جِدِّيَّة, then أَنْزَعِيَّة, then قَائِمِيَّة, then جُسِّيَّة, then أَحَدِيَّة, then صَمَدِيَّة — and so up to إِلَهِيَّة, and at the very top, هُوِيَّة. The last and highest rank is the Ipseity, the rank of the bare "He." Ten ranks in all are set out this way, ascending from the Imamate of spirituality up to the Ipseity, mapping the whole ladder of stations by which the soul climbs back toward where it came from.

One thing remains, and it grows straight out of the word at the center of all this — *mashfu*, the "paired" or "coupled" sin. That word *shafa*, which means a pairing, carries among the دُعَاة a hidden referent, and so do its two companions, *witr* and *julus*. All three are borrowed from the language of prayer. The *shafa* prayer is the paired one, of two *rakat* (رَكْعَات). The *witr* is the single, odd *rakat*. The *julus* is the prayer of two *rakat* performed sitting. And each of these has its inner meaning, its *taweel*. The referent of *shafa*, the paired prayer, is the Prophet — peace and blessings be upon him — together with Lady Fatima, for they are the noble pair. The referent of *witr*, the single prayer, is Imam Ali, peace be upon him, the odd and singular one. And the referent of *julus*, the sitting prayer of two *rakat*, is Imam Hasan and Imam Husayn together. It is told that Imam Husayn himself, at Karbala, would name these very correspondences — that the referent of *shafa* is the Prophet, that the referent of *witr* was his own father, and so on — and the text affirms:

وَتِلْكَ آيَةٌ وَاحِدَةٌ

> "And these together are one sign."

So the very terminology by which the دُعَاة name this "coupled sin" of inadequate speech opens, in its own turn, onto the hidden ranks of the Prophet and his pure household. The word reached for to confess our poverty before God turns out to carry, folded inside it, the names of the ones through whom He is approached. The matter does not rest here. What has been shown is this: why He is named and why the naming must be pardoned; the ladder climbed to its highest rung, with the bare "He" waiting at the top; and now this last word has handed over, almost unnoticed, the household by which the ascent is actually made. The pronoun pointed us upward. These names tell us by what hands the letter is carried.

The realities this teaching unveils ascend by degrees, each standing a little higher than the one before. This matter opens with a saying handed down from the حُدُود, the ranks of the spiritual hierarchy, upon whom be peace:

> إِنَّ التَّوْحِيدَ هُوَ مَعْرِفَةُ الْحُدُودِ، وَالتَّنْزِيهَ نَفْيُ الْإِلَهِيَّةِ عَنْهُمْ، وَالتَّجْرِيدَ سَلْبُ الْأَسْمَاءِ وَالصِّفَاتِ عَنِ اللَّهِ تَعَالَى
>
> "Verily, Tawhid is the gnosis of the ranks; and tanzih is the negation of divinity from them; and tajrid is the divestment of the names and attributes from God the Exalted."

And at once he adds that this is a summarized statement.

Something is being corrected here, at the very floor of everything. Asked what Tawhid is, most answer almost before the question is finished: it means to consider God as one. But that is not what the حُدُود teach, and on reflection it cannot be. To count God as one is already to have placed Him under number — and whatever can be numbered as one can in principle be numbered as two, as three, or reckoned as a part of one. So to declare God "one" in that sense is not Tawhid at all. It is *shirk* (الشِّرْك), the gravest of all errors, because it lays a definition and a measure across the One who admits of no definition and no measure. He cannot be called one. He cannot be called two. He cannot be called three. He cannot be called a part of one. No number reaches Him. No boundary can be drawn around Him.

What, then, is Tawhid? It is *marifat al-hudud* — the gnosis of the ranks. This is the cornerstone of the entire teaching. To affirm the divine unity is to recognize each *had*, each rank of the spiritual hierarchy, as utterly unique — *yekta* — in its own place. It is not to declare God unique. It is to know that every rank is unique in its proper station, and to attain the gnosis of exactly where that rank stands: at what level, in what station, in what relation to the ranks above it and below it. God is not the one being called unique here. Rather, every *had* is singular in its own place, and the gnosis of that singularity — of that whole ordered hierarchy of distinct ranks — is what the word Tawhid actually carries. This is the greatest thing a person can know: the Tawhid of the حُدُود, the recognition that every rank is singular and irreplaceable in its own degree.

These ranks did not drift into their positions by accident. God created the حُدُود and granted each of them authority — *ikhtiyar* (اَلْاِخْتِيَار) — and said, in effect: use your powers. Each *had*, according to its own nature and likeness, was given a share of power and the freedom to exercise it. From the differences that grew out of how each one used that share, the whole arrangement, the *tartib* of the hierarchy, settled into place. It is the way the load-bearing walls of a building, once set, decide where every room and doorway can fall. To know that arrangement — to understand by what gradation one rank stands above or below another — is Tawhid. The hierarchy is not pressed down on the ranks from outside. It is the very expression of how each one used the authority entrusted to it.

It follows that Tawhid has levels, because not everyone can take in the whole of it at once. The Prophet himself, peace and blessings upon him, pointed to this when he said:

> مَا عَرَفَنِي إِلَّا اللَّهُ وَأَنَا
>
> "None has known me except God, and I myself."

As a person's own station — his *martaba* — rises, the depth of his Tawhid rises with it. There are many stations of Tawhid, each answering to the elevation of the one who knows. A question then opens: how many beings' Tawhid can a single person actually perform across the whole span of a life? The answer is what fixes the rank of this science above every other. The knowledge of Tawhid is *ajall al-ilm* — the highest knowledge of all. To recognize the station of each and every rank, to know precisely where each one stands, is the most exalted of all knowing.

The reason it is the highest follows from how boundless its object is. The body offers a way in. Within it there are some three hundred and sixty parts, and each organ, each member, has its own quality and its own degree of excellence — one finer than another. To have full gnosis of the body would mean knowing each of these parts in its proper rank and worth. That same demand, lifted to the whole order of existence, is what the true Tawhid asks. Every being — every *zawat* — that God the Exalted created, and they are beyond counting, passed through its stages until it reached *kamal-e insani*, human perfection. The real *marifat*, the true Tawhid, is to know each of these beings: when and how it arrived at its human perfection, at what station it now stands, and how it stands in relation to all the rest. That is the very limit of gnosis. Because God created innumerable beings, the gnosis that answers to them is likewise innumerable, and the intellect is simply left staggered before the immensity of what there is to know. As much as one is able to attain, one attains — and no more.

Out of that immensity comes something sober and entirely practical for anyone walking this road. For salvation — *najat* — the question is exactly this: which of the ranks' gnosis does a person manage to acquire, and how much of it? As much gnosis as a person attains within a lifetime, by that measure his station, his *martaba*, will be established. And according to that station, the corresponding hierarchy will be set in place within his هَيْكَل, his spiritual form. It is through knowledge — *ilm* — and action — عَمَل — working together that the arrangement inside the هَيْكَل is built. A person's eventual rank in the spiritual world is not handed to him arbitrarily. It is the precise measure of the gnosis he attained and enacted in this life. And what, in the end, is salvation itself? It is *khatima bil-khair*, a good end. To finish well, to close one's life upon the good — that is salvation, and that good end is itself the fruit of the gnosis and the action gathered along the way.

Here a delicate question presses in. Is gnosis attained by one's own doing, or is it made to happen to a person? The teaching holds both at once and refuses to let go of either. The effort a person expends — his *juhd* — genuinely earns him gnosis; he really does strive, and he really does acquire. But onto that effort there also descends the grace — the *fazl* — of those who stand above him, so that gnosis is also made to happen to him, bestowed from a higher hand. Neither one is enough by itself. There is the labor that is a person's to perform, and there is the grace that is given from above, and gnosis is the place where the two meet.

The word حُدُود itself carries something more. A *had* is a limit. Every rank has its limit, a boundary it cannot pass beyond, and to know that limit — the final point of ascent, the *nuqta-e irtifa* to which a given rank rises — is itself part of the gnosis of the ranks. So the limit of the Prophet's ascent, peace and blessings upon him, is *Hijabiyyat*, the station of being a veil. The limit of Lady Fatimah is *Hujjiyyat*, the station of the *Hujjah*, the proof. The final point of Abd al-Muttalib is *Jaddiyyat*, the station of the *Jadd* — and *Jaddiyyat* is not a single point but comprises ten stations, ten *maratib*, so that one must know further at which of those ten degrees a particular individual is found, the seventh standing lower and the higher being something other than it. To attain the gnosis of these limits, and of the gradations folded inside each one, is a very great science indeed. This is Tawhid.

The opening saying named three things, not one, and each must be taken in turn, for Tawhid in its full statement has three branches. The first is Tawhid itself, already laid down: *marifat al-hudud*, the gnosis of the ranks.

The second branch is تَنْزِيه. The saying defines it as *nafyi al-ilahiyyat anhum* — the negation of divinity from the ranks. To perform تَنْزِيه is to declare transcendent, to declare pure, and specifically to deny that divinity resides in the حُدُود. There is no divinity in the ranks; the attribute of creating, of bringing beings into existence, is not theirs. But exactness about what *ilahiyyat*, divinity, means here matters, because the word *ilah* carries more than one sense. What is intended in this place is *ibda (إبداع) al-zawat*, the origination of beings — the power to bring a being into existence out of nothing. *Tanzih* strips that power away from the ranks: not one of them, the saying insists, possesses the power of *ibda-e zawat*, the origination of a being. Not even the First Intellect, the *Aql al-Awwal*, possesses it. Every one of them, without a single exception, is itself created — *paida kiye hue* — and the created cannot originate. A second meaning of *ilah* — the sense in which a higher rank becomes, for the one who stands bewildered before it, a kind of "god" — is set aside for the present. For now the sense that تَنْزِيه needs is this: the creating power belongs to none of the ranks, and so divinity, in the sense of origination, must be negated from them all.

The third branch is تَجْرِيد, defined as *salb al-asmai wa al-sifati an Allah Taala* — the divestment of the names and the attributes from God the Exalted. The root of تَجْرِيد is the stripping of bark from a tree, and that is precisely the image: to strip away from God every name and every attribute, because no name can truly be predicated of Him. Even the name "Allah" cannot, in the strictest sense, truly be His — for it too is a name, and He is beyond all names. So out of sheer necessity one is reduced to calling Him "Hu," "He" — and even in saying "Hu" a person confesses his own helplessness. O God, we have no words. To affirm even our own existence we are forced to address You somehow — but by what name shall we call You? This is the predicament caught in the phrase:

> ذَنْبٌ مَشْفُوعٌ بِالِاسْتِغْفَارِ
>
> "A sin coupled with a plea for forgiveness."

The very act of naming Him is a kind of sin — and yet it is a sin that arrives already accompanied by its own forgiveness. For man is helpless. He must call upon God by some name, because if he did not, he would in effect be denying that the Existent exists at all. To turn toward the existence of God he must address Him; to address Him he must name Him; and in naming Him he commits the fault. But the *istighfar* (اِسْتِغْفَار), the plea for pardon, is built into the act itself — because God the Exalted understands the helplessness of His servant. He knows the servant owns no word adequate to call upon Him, and that by whatever name the servant calls, that calling will be accepted, and the forgiveness granted along with it. So تَجْرِيد is the negation, from God the Exalted, of all the names and all the attributes whatsoever that might be ascribed to Him.

This whole three-branched saying is *qawlun mujmalun* — a summary, an encompassing statement that now stands in need of detailed exposition. The exposition begins by opening a division within the gnosis of the ranks itself:

> لِأَنَّ الْمَعْرِفَةَ بِالْحُدُودِ مَعْرِفَتَانِ: مَعْرِفَةٌ ظَاهِرَةٌ يُعْرَفُ بِهَا شَخْصُ الْحَدِّ وَمَقَامُهُ، وَهَذِهِ الْمَعْرِفَةُ يَتَسَاوَى فِيهَا الْوَلِيُّ وَغَيْرُهُ مِنَ الْأَضْدَادِ وَالطُّغَاةِ؛ وَمَعْرِفَةٌ بَاطِنَةٌ يَخْتَصُّ بِهَا أَهْلُ الْمَعَارِفِ مِنْ أَهْلِ الْحَقِّ، وَهُوَ ابْتِدَاءُ وُجُودِ الْحَدِّ
>
> "Because the gnosis of the ranks is of two kinds of gnosis: an outer gnosis, by which the person of the rank and his station are known, and in which the friend and others among the adversaries and the tyrants stand equal; and an inner gnosis, special to the people of gnosis from among the people of truth — and it is the beginning of the existence of the rank."

So the gnosis of the ranks is of two kinds. The first is the outer gnosis, the *marifah (الْمَعْرِفَة) zahirah*, by which the person of a rank and his station are recognized — the knowledge of who a given rank is and where he stands. Its distinguishing mark is this: in the outer gnosis the friend, the *wali* (وَلِيّ), and the adversary stand on perfectly equal footing. The lover, the enemy, and the indifferent stranger all perceive the same outward person. All of them see how tall he is, how many feet in height; whether his face is round, whether he wears a beard; what his hands are like, what his feet are like. The devoted disciple sees exactly this, and the bitter enemy sees exactly this, and in that respect there is no difference between them at all. The outer gnosis is not trivial — it too is hard to attain in its fullness. But its mark is that in it friend and foe are made equal, because it reaches only the outward person and his station.

The second kind, far higher, is the inner gnosis — the *marifah batinah* — and this one is reserved to the people of gnosis, the *ahl al-maarif*, from among the people of truth, the *ahl al-haqq* (أَهْلُ الْحَقّ). What is its object? It is *ibtida wujud al-had* — the very beginning of the existence of the rank. When did the existence of a given *had* begin? These ranks that were created — where were they created, and from whom? Here, in compressed form, opens the long and difficult account of how the ranks came to be. The حُدُود were brought into being where the *fatahun* were — those whose sins were few — and then they were called. A first call went out, and at that first call they did not confess; a second call was made, and a third, and a fourth; in each room they were summoned in turn, the way a sealed message is carried from chamber to chamber before it is finally opened — and one must know in which room each rank finally made its confession. This is a very long account, and its full telling lies beyond the present matter. But the point that matters now is this: the gnosis of that beginning — of where, and from whom, and through how many summons a rank came into being — is precisely the inner gnosis, and the gnosis of such a thing belongs to the Imam of the Age, the إِمَام الزَّمَان, upon him be peace.

The inner gnosis does not stop at the beginning. It comprises also *ghayatuhu*, the rank's end, and *ila ayna maaduhu wa nihayatuhu* — where its return, its *maad*, and its final terminus lie. To know the inner reality of a *had* is to know the entire arc of its essence, its *khamira*: at what point that essence was first established, and at what level a person was standing when he passed out of this world. Was he in the ninth degree of the *Mumin*, or the eighth, or the seventh? Did he climb from *Mumin* to become a مُكَثِّر, and from مُكَثِّر to become a *Madhun*? At precisely which station did his existence come to rest, and to what return is it bound? This is a gnosis of extreme difficulty, and neither its steepness nor its stakes are to be softened. It cannot be reached except by the *murtazin*, the disciplined ones, and the *muhiqqin*, the verifiers — those who have purified themselves and proven the truth within themselves. And then comes a word of the utmost severity: for one whose gnosis of this inner reality is deficient, there is no Tawhid at all. Without the inner knowledge of the beginning, the level, and the return of a rank's essence, a man may hold no true Tawhid whatsoever.

So something of this matter is set down here — opened, as far as it can be opened — as a help to the brethren in the gnosis of the Tawhid of God the Exalted. The inner gnosis has named its price and named its reward; what remains is to begin, carefully, to enter it.

chapters.chapter_key: the nearest rank: breaking the self to climb
chapters.before_md:
With the help of God, glory be to Him, and under the gaze of His friend upon His earth, peace be upon him — the price has been named and the reward has been named. Now the door opens, one foot after the other, for this is learned only by entering it.

> فَأَقُولُ بِعَوْنِ اللَّهِ سُبْحَانَهُ وَلَحَظَاتِ وَلِيِّهِ فِي أَرْضِهِ، سَلَامُ اللَّهِ عَلَيْهِ، إِنَّ أَقْرَبَ الْحُدُودِ إِلَيْنَا هُوَ الْمُكَاثِرُ وَمَا ثَبَتَ مِنَ الْقَوْلِ فِي الدَّانِي مِنَ الْحُدُودِ ثَبَتَ فِي الْعَالِي.
>
> "So I say, with the help of God, glory be to Him, and the glances of His Wali upon His earth, peace of God be upon him: verily the closest of the ranks to us is the Mukathir, and what is established of the saying regarding the lower of the ranks is established for the higher."

That single breath carries two things, and everything that follows rests on them. The first: the rank nearest to a person — the one through which an ordinary man makes his first true contact with the spiritual order — is the Mukathir. The second is a rule of proportion that governs all that follows. Whatever is established for the lower rank is established, in its own measure, for the higher. What holds of the Mukathir holds, raised to its degree, of the Madhun, the Dai Mutlaq, the Dai Mahsur, and every rank above him. A single law of load-bearing runs through every floor of a building: proven for the ground floor, it is proven, in proportion, for the floors that rest upon it. And it runs in both directions, for a higher rank carries the lower one within himself. A Madhun is also a Mukathir in his own place — and was a Mukathir before he was ever a Madhun.

But the Mukathir cannot be reached in a single step. Below the ranks proper lie two thresholds that must first be crossed. The first is the Mustajib, the responder — literally, the one who accepts. The Mustajib is the one who takes the noble pledge, the ahd sharif, saying with his tongue, "I accept the noble pledge," whether or not his heart and his deeds have yet caught up with his tongue. That is his defining mark: the profession on the tongue. He affirms, "the Imam of this time is such," and binds himself by that word. The Mustajib has ten levels, graded by hiddat — the intensity, the sharpness, the keenness of gaze with which the pledge is taken. Some come to the pledge the way a man drifts into a marriage, casually, half-attending. Others take it with the burning intensity of a Sayyidna Jafar. The Imam himself takes the pledge. According to the intensity of the one pledging, his level is fixed — and so there are ten degrees of the noble pledge.

The second threshold is the Mumin, the believer. The classical definition holds its three parts together:

> الْقَوْلُ بِاللِّسَانِ وَالتَّصْدِيقُ بِالْجَنَانِ وَالْعَمَلُ بِالْأَرْكَانِ
>
> "Profession with the tongue, affirmation with the heart, and action with the limbs."

The Mumin is the one in whom all three have joined: he professes with his tongue, he affirms inwardly in his heart, and he acts outwardly with his limbs. He too has ten levels of his own. Here a distinction holds firm: neither the Mustajib nor the Mumin belongs to the hudud. They stand below the ranks proper — the necessary thresholds crossed on the approach to the hierarchy, but not yet part of it. Only after these, only with the Mukathir, does one truly step inside.

With the Mukathir the threshold is crossed. He is the first rank within the hudud, the first degree of the spiritual order, and it is exactly this rank that the Prophet's transmitted saying placed nearest. The word itself reveals what he is. Mukathir comes from kasr, breaking — for the Mukathir is the one who breaks his opponent with his proofs, his hujjat. But whom does he break first? Not the man before him. He must first break his own self. This is kasr-e nafs, the breaking of the self, and there is no beginning without it.

To perform kasr-e nafs is to put every word, every deed, and every intention through one relentless examination. The self must ask: Is what I am about to say in line with the command of God and His Prophet? Is the deed I am about to do in line with their command? Is the very thought now crossing my mind in line with the command of God and His Prophet? To bind oneself entirely to that single measure — to become a captive of the command in speech, in action, and in thought alike — that is what it means to be a Mukathir.

The logic is exacting. Only the man who has broken his own self can break another. If he has set himself in order in this matter, his proofs can break the one who stands before him. But if he could not break his own self — indulging it instead, telling it this is allowed and that is allowed, handing himself a license here and an excuse there — then how is he to break anyone else? He has no standing to do it. From this comes a hard requirement. For the Mukathir, the acquisition of the sciences, the ulum, is not optional; it is indispensable. Without knowledge no Mukathir is ever formed, for he must first know the command of God and His Prophet in order to test himself against it. Only once he knows the command can he recognize that some word of his fell short of it, that some deed of his swerved from it, that some thought of his strayed from it. Having judged and broken himself by that knowledge, he is then fit to break the man before him with his proofs. And by the rule already set down — what is fixed for the lower is fixed for the higher — this same description holds, each at his proper degree, for the Mukathir, the Madhun, the Dai Mutlaq, the Dai Mahsur, and every rank of the hudud above.

A real difficulty rises here. If the Mukathir is flesh and bone like everyone else, what actually separates him from the ordinary man beside him? The matter is stated thus:

> وَذَلِكَ أَنَّهُ وَإِنْ كَانَ يَجْمَعُهُ وَغَيْرَهُ مِنَ الْأَشْخَاصِ الْإِنْسَانِيَّةِ الْحُدُودُ وَالْأَقْطَارُ وَكَوْنُهُمَا جَمِيعًا مِنْ لَحْمٍ وَدَمٍ وَعِظَامٍ وَأَعْصَابٍ وَعُرُوقٍ وَغَيْرِ ذَلِكَ فَلَيْسَ بِسَوَاءٍ.
>
> "And that is because, although he and others from among the human persons are gathered by the limits and the regions, and although both of them are entirely of flesh and blood and bones and nerves and veins and other than that, yet they are not the same."

The Mukathir and the ordinary man are gathered inside the same limits, the same hudud, the same regions, the same aqtar — the same boundaries of body and place hold them both. Both are made of flesh, both of blood, both of bones, nerves, veins, and all the rest. Set side by side and inspected from the outside, they show no difference: this one is flesh and bone, that one is flesh and bone. And yet they are not the same. Beneath an identical outward composition lies an immense difference. The matter is resolved thus:

> لِأَنَّ هَذَا الْحَدَّ الَّذِي هُوَ الْمُكَاثِرُ قَدْ تَلَطَّفَ مِزَاجُهُ وَصَفَا جَوْهَرُهُ وَهَذَا صُعُودًا مَرَاتِبَ جُمَّةً.
>
> "Because this rank, which is the Mukathir, his temperament has become refined and his essence has become pure, and this through ascending many stations."

The difference is not merely inward; it reaches even into the outward. The Mukathir's temperament has been refined — talattafa mizajuhu — and his essence made pure — safa jawharuhu. His flesh is no longer common flesh, his blood no longer common blood. Everything of his has been transformed, and transformed even outwardly, though no one around him perceived it and the ignorant could not begin to discern it. And how did this come about? He climbed through stations upon stations that others never reached. The passage continues:

> وَتَقَرَّبَ بِهَا فَتَقَرَّبَ بِهَا مِنَ الْمَبْدَإِ الْأَوَّلِ حَتَّى صَارَ فِي أَعْلَى مَرَاتِبِ الْإِنْسَانِيَّةِ الَّتِي هِيَ أَوَّلُ رُتَبِ الْمَلَكُوتِيَّةِ.
>
> "And he drew near through that, drawing near through it to the first principle, until he reached the highest stations of humanity, which are the first of the spiritual ranks."

Through that refinement and that ascent he has drawn close to the first principle, al-mabda al-awwal — close, that is, to the very source his creation came out of, so that he now stands near to returning to it. He has reached the highest stations of the human, and those highest human stations are themselves the first of the spiritual ranks, awwalu rutab al-malakutiyya. The image is of a staircase between two floors: the topmost stair of the lower floor is, at the same time, the first stair of the floor above. The summit of the human is the threshold of the malakut, the spiritual world, and the Mukathir stands exactly on that joining-stair — where the highest rung of the human order is also the lowest rung of the angelic.

From that height comes the most exalted thing said of him:

> وَهُوَ مَهْبِطٌ لِوَحْيِ اللَّهِ وَبَيْتٌ مِنْ بُيُوتِهِ.
>
> "And he is a place of descent for the revelation of God, and a house from His houses."

He is the mahbat — the landing-place — for the wahy, the revelation of God; the very ground upon which revelation alights. And he is a bayt, a house, from among the houses of God. Why is he so? Because in his every thought he kept the command of God and His Prophet before him; in his every word he kept that command before him; in his every deed he kept it before him. Having made that command the standing presence of his thinking, his speaking, and his acting, he became a house from the houses of God, a place fit for revelation to descend upon. This is anchored in the Book itself:

> فِي بُيُوتٍ أَذِنَ اللَّهُ أَن تُرْفَعَ وَيُذْكَرَ فِيهَا اسْمُهُ يُسَبِّحُ لَهُ فِيهَا بِالْغُدُوِّ وَالْآصَالِ
>
> "In houses which God has permitted to be exalted and His name to be remembered therein; in them He is glorified in the mornings and the evenings."

> ثُمَّ حَقَّقَ فِي الْآيَةِ أَنَّ الْبُيُوتَ هُمُ الْحُدُودُ.
>
> "Then He established in the verse that the houses are the ranks."

So the "houses" of the verse — the ones God permitted to be exalted, within which His name is remembered and glorified morning and evening — are, in their inner meaning, the hudud, the ranks of the hierarchy, of whom the Mukathir is the first. And the verse continues:

> رِجَالٌ لَّا تُلْهِيهِمْ تِجَارَةٌ وَلَا بَيْعٌ عَن ذِكْرِ اللَّهِ وَإِقَامِ الصَّلَاةِ وَإِيتَاءِ الزَّكَاةِ
>
> "Men whom neither commerce nor sale diverts from the remembrance of God and the establishing of prayer and the giving of zakat."

> يُرِيدُ إِقَامَةَ الدَّعْوَةِ
>
> "By which He intends the establishing of the dawah."

Those "men whom neither commerce nor sale diverts from the remembrance of God, the establishing of prayer, and the giving of zakat" are these same ranks. And what is meant here by their establishing of prayer is, in its inner sense, iqamat al-dawah — the establishing of the divine summons, the dawah. The verse's outward language of trade and selling is illuminated by the parallel passage in Surah al-Jumuah:

> يَا أَيُّهَا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا إِذَا نُودِيَ لِلصَّلَاةِ مِن يَوْمِ الْجُمُعَةِ فَاسْعَوْا إِلَىٰ ذِكْرِ اللَّهِ وَذَرُوا الْبَيْعَ ۚ ذَٰلِكُمْ خَيْرٌ لَّكُمْ إِن كُنتُمْ تَعْلَمُونَ ۝ فَإِذَا قُضِيَتِ الصَّلَاةُ فَانتَشِرُوا فِي الْأَرْضِ وَابْتَغُوا مِن فَضْلِ اللَّهِ وَاذْكُرُوا اللَّهَ كَثِيرًا لَّعَلَّكُمْ تُفْلِحُونَ
>
> "O you who believe, when the call is proclaimed for the prayer on the day of Jumuah, hasten to the remembrance of God and leave off trade. That is better for you, if you only knew. And when the prayer is concluded, disperse in the land and seek of the bounty of God, and remember God much, that you may be successful."

Those whom the commerce and the buying and selling of the world cannot divert from the remembrance of God, from the establishing of prayer, from the giving of zakat — they are the very ones who, in the inner sense, establish the dawah.

Once the establishing of prayer is seen to mean the establishing of the dawah, a wider door opens. Every pillar, every obligation of the religion carries an inner meaning, a taweel, beneath its outward form — the way a sealed letter passes through several hands before it reaches the one it was written for, each outward act delivering an inner sense to those fit to read it. These may be set out one by one.

Wilayat, in its inner sense, is to repent in the world of motes — to turn back in repentance in that primordial world of the smallest particles of being. Taharat, purity, is to cleanse oneself of the filth of Iblis through the knowledge of the Tenth. Salat, prayer, is to act upon the commands of the Tenth — or of whichever Imam in whose sphere one has arrived and whose dawah has reached him — to carry out the commands he has given. This is exactly why, when the prayer is established, the announcement is "the prayer has stood," qad qamat al-salah, for qiyam means to stand, and the standing of the prayer is the standing-up to enact the command. Zakat is to give out a portion of the knowledge one has been given: once the knowledge received reaches a certain measure, a small portion of it becomes obligatory to dispense. This mirrors material zakat exactly. In the outward law there is zakat al-fitra, owed by every single person, and there is zakat al-mal, which falls due only when wealth has piled up to its threshold. So it is with the zakat of knowledge. Some sciences are owed by nature to every person and must be explained to all, like the fitra. Others, like the zakat on accumulated wealth, are owed only once one's store of knowledge has grown to the level that makes a portion of it obligatory to give out.

The inner meanings continue. Sawm, fasting, is to conceal knowledge — to withhold it from the undeserving, to keep it hidden from those unfit to receive it. Khums, the fifth, is to give out a fifth part of any knowledge that comes unexpectedly. In the outward law, when some windfall or booty reaches a man that he was not expecting, a fifth of it is due. Hazrat Imam Husayn, peace be upon him, used every month to set aside the khums even of his own salary, reasoning that he had not expected such money to come to him, and so he gave out its fifth. It is the same with knowledge. If some knowledge descends unexpectedly, from the saints of God, its fifth part must be given out. When knowledge and virtues descended upon Imam Husayn, what did he do with their fifth? He propagated it, he made the matter plain, he gave the fifth away; the remaining four parts were his own by right, but the fifth he dispensed. Hajj is al-qasdu ila bayt Allah, the setting-out toward the House of God — and the House of God, inwardly, is the Imam al-Zaman, peace be upon him, who is the place of God; the "house" is the bab al-batin, the inner gate, and hajj is to ready one's whole form and bearing, with a true heart, and set out toward that inner gate. And jihad is to take one's own self — no, not merely to take it, but to sacrifice it, to slay it — in the way of God, when the command comes from the Imam al-Zaman to offer up the self. The greatest jihad is the slaying of the commanding self, the nafs, so that the true hero, the lion of the field, is the man who has killed within himself that great beast which is his own commanding soul.

Then the verse is sealed:

> يُرِيدُ إِقَامَةَ الدَّعْوَةِ الَّتِي هِيَ مَنْصُورُ الصَّلَاةِ الظَّاهِرَةِ وَلَا قِوَامَ لَهَا إِلَّا بِهَا.
>
> "He intends the establishing of the dawah, which is the object supported by the outward prayer, and the dawah has no standing except through it."

What God intends by the verse is the establishing of the dawah — the very object that the outward prayer serves and holds up. And the dawah itself has no strength, no standing, except through that prayer. The outer prayer and the inner dawah are bound to each other, each holding the other upright, the way a river first finds its channel before it can carry water to the field: were the channel cut, the water would have nowhere to run.

The contrast that gives this whole teaching its weight is a warning grave enough to stir fear. Set against the Mukathir is the man who does not establish prayer:

> وَغَيْرُهُ مِنْ هَذِهِ الْأَشْخَاصِ الْإِنْسَانِيَّةِ وَإِنْ كَانَ عَلَى الْحَالَةِ الَّتِي هُوَ عَلَيْهَا فَإِنَّ مِزَاجَهُ غَيْرُ مُتَلَطِّفٍ وَجَوْهَرَهُ غَيْرُ صَافٍ وَشَخْصَهُ سَائِرٌ فِي الِانْحِدَارِ وَالْبُعْدِ مِنَ الْمَبْدَإِ الْأَوَّلِ سَائِرٌ فِي آخِرِ رُتَبِ الْإِنْسَانِيَّةِ مُقَهْقَرًا إِلَى مَا دُونَهُ مِنَ الصُّوَرِ الْأَلْفِيَّةِ.
>
> "And other than him, of these human persons — even though he is in the same state in which the Mukathir is — his temperament is unrefined and his essence impure, and his person is proceeding in decline and in distance from the first principle, proceeding toward the last of the human ranks, pushed back to what is below it of the thousand-fold forms."

This "other than him" is the man who is not a Mukathir — the ordinary man, or the opponent. Outwardly he stands in the very same state, on the very same platform, as the Mukathir. Both are flesh and blood. Both wear the same human form. Both arrived in the same world. And yet their paths run opposite. The Mukathir is going up; this other man is going down. One draws near to the first principle; the other moves away from it. They are gathered on one platform, and from that single point one walks this way and the other that — one of them going to the cinema and one of them to the mosque, setting out together from the same spot. What decides it is the establishing of prayer. Where iqamat al-salah does not happen — where a man does not establish the inward prayer, and in that case does not even establish the outward one — he moves away from the first principle, declining toward the last of the human ranks, pushed back, muqahqaran, beneath even the lowest of them.

And the descent does not stop there:

> الَّتِي هِيَ أَضَلُّ سَبِيلًا مِنَ الْأَنْعَامِ إِلَى الصِّرَاطِ الْمُعْوَجِّ مُنْتَهِيًا فِيهِ إِلَى بَرْزَخِ الْخَوْفِ.
>
> "Which is more astray in its path than the cattle, onto the crooked path, ending therein at the isthmus of fear."

The man who fails to establish prayer is driven below the thousand-fold form, the surat al-alfiyya, until he becomes more astray in his path than the cattle, turned onto the crooked path, the sirat al-muawwaj, ending at last in the barzakh al-khawf, the isthmus of fear. Step by step he proceeds toward that dreadful end. Here the prayer rises: may God keep us, and all our brethren, far from such a fate, for the sake of the master of the prophets, peace and blessings be upon him and his pure progeny, the blessings of God upon them all. The picture stands exactly so. Two men of identical outward make, set on one platform — one establishing the inward prayer and so becoming a Mukathir who ascends, the other establishing neither inward nor even outward prayer, his temperament and his deeds so hardened that he descends. The same flesh, the same blood, the same world — and opposite ends, because of one thing: the establishing, or the abandoning, of prayer.

And this is no strange or singular law. The same pattern, and a proof of it, appears down in the animal kingdom:

> وَفِي الْأَشْخَاصِ الْحَيَوَانِيَّةِ عِبْرَةٌ لِمَنِ اعْتَبَرَ وَبَصِيرَةٌ لِمَنْ تَبَصَّرَ وَتَدَبَّرَ.
>
> "And in the animal forms there is a lesson for one who takes a lesson, and insight for one who reflects and contemplates."

In the animal figures — and "person" here means figure, not human person — there is a lesson for whoever will take a lesson, and insight for whoever will reflect and contemplate. The argument runs thus:

> وَذَلِكَ أَنَّ الْبَهَائِمَ الْمُحَلَّلَةَ مِنَ الْبَقَرِ وَالْغَنَمِ وَالْإِبِلِ وَغَيْرِ ذَلِكَ مُتَمَاثِلَةٌ فِي الْخَلْقِ هِيَ وَالسِّبَاعُ الْمُحَرَّمَةُ لِكَوْنِهِمْ جَمِيعًا مِنْ لَحْمٍ وَدَمٍ وَعِظَامٍ وَأَعْصَابٍ وَعُرُوقٍ وَبَشَرٍ وَجِلْدٍ وَوَبَرٍ غَيْرَ أَنَّ الْبَهَائِمَ قَدْ صَارَتْ غِذَاءً لِلْإِنْسَانِ.
>
> "And that is because the lawful animals — of cattle and sheep and camels and the like — are similar in creation to the forbidden predatory animals, both being of flesh and blood and bones and nerves and veins and skin and hide and fur; except that the lawful animals have become food for the human being."

The lawful animals — the cow, the sheep, the camel, and their kind — are identical in their outward creation to the forbidden beasts of prey, the siba. Both are flesh, blood, bones, nerves, veins, skin, hide, and fur; in their physical make there is no difference between them. And yet they are not the same, and the proof of the difference lies in how each stands toward man. The lawful animals have become food for the human being — for that human who is the caliph of God upon His earth. And so:

> مُسْتَأْنِسَةً إِلَيْهِ سَائِرَةً إِلَى الصُّعُودِ وَالتَّرَقِّي فِي الصِّرَاطِ السَّوِيِّ الَّذِي هُوَ الشَّخْصُ الْبَشَرِيُّ قَرِيبَةً مِنَ الْمَبْدَإِ الْأَوَّلِ.
>
> "Taking intimacy with him, proceeding toward ascent and progress upon the straight path, which is the human person, near to the first principle."

The lawful animals take intimacy with man; they come close to him, become his food, and by becoming part of the human they proceed toward ascent and progress upon the straight path, the sirat al-sawiyy. And what is the straight path here? It is the human person himself — the sirat al-mustaqim is the bashari, the human form, which stands near to the first principle that is the origin and the return. The lawful animal, eaten and taken up into the human who is the caliph of God, ascends through him toward the source. The predatory animals are the reverse:

> وَالسِّبَاعُ نَافِرَةٌ عَنِ الْإِنْسَانِ مُعَادِيَةٌ لَهُ سَائِرَةً فِي الِانْحِدَارِ سَائِرَةً إِلَى الْبُعْدِ الْأَبْعَدِ مِنَ الْمَبْدَإِ الْأَوَّلِ.
>
> "And the predatory animals are averse to the human, hostile to him, proceeding in decline, proceeding to the furthest distance from the first principle."

The forbidden beasts of prey shy away from man and are hostile to him; they do not draw near to become his food and so they do not ascend through him, but proceed in decline, moving ever farther from the first principle. So although the two kinds of animal are made of one and the same stuff, the conclusion stands:

> فَلَيْسُوا بِسَوَاءٍ فِي هَذِهِ الظَّوَاهِرِ وَالْخَلْقِ الْمُشْتَرَكِ وَكَذَلِكَ الطَّائِعُونَ وَالْعُصَاةُ وَالْبَاعِدُ أَبْعَدُ مِنْ ذَلِكَ.
>
> "So they are not equal in these outward appearances and shared creation; and likewise the obedient and the disobedient — and the distance is greater still."

They are not equal, for all their shared outward look and common creation. And it is just so with men. The lawful animal that ascends through its intimacy with man is like the Mukathir, the purified human who rises toward the first principle. The forbidden beast that flees man and falls away is like the man who declines.
