So among human beings the obedient — the muti, the tai — and the disobedient, the asi, though they too share one platform, one composition, one world, are separated by a distance greater even than the one that divides the two kinds of beast. One rises and one descends, and between them lies the whole interval between the first principle and the furthest distance from it.

The joining-stair has now been reached, where the highest human station opens onto the first of the spiritual ranks; what the Mukathir broke in himself to climb there, and what the man beside him failed to break, has been shown. The threshold is named, the ascent is named, the descent is named. What waits is the next of the ranks — and it can be reached only by the same road the Mukathir went: through the self, broken first.

chapters.chapter_key: every teacher a threshold, not a god
chapters.before_md:
The man who broke himself at the threshold climbed, and what became of him after the climb is quieter and stranger than the climb itself. It concerns not what he gained but what he became. The soul of the مُكَثِّر — the one who has outstripped the others and stands at the summit of the human ranks — was changed by the road he traveled.

> وَإِذَا كَانَ ذَلِكَ كَذَلِكَ فَإِنَّ نَفْسَ الْحَدِّ الَّذِي هُوَ الْمُكَاثِرُ قَدْ تَلَطَّفَتْ وَصَفَتْ وَعَلَتْ بِارْتِفَاعِ الصِّفَاتِ الْمَوْضُوعَةِ لَهَا وَعُلُوِّهِ، ثُمَّ اتَّصَلَ بِهَا مِنَ الْعُلُومِ الْإِلَهِيَّةِ وَالْأَسْرَارِ الْمَلَكُوتِيَّةِ مَا أَحْكَمَهَا صَفَاءً كُلِّيًّا وَأَلْطَفَهَا تَلْطِيفًا مَلَكُوتِيًّا وَصَبَغَهَا صِبْغَةً إِلَهِيَّةً وَأَشْرَقَهَا وَجَوْهَرَهَا وَأَشَفَّهَا
>
> "And since the matter is so, then the soul of the rank which is the Mukathir has become refined and pure and elevated through the elevation of its established attributes and its loftiness; then there connected with it, of the divine sciences and spiritual secrets, that which perfected it with a universal purity, and refined it with a spiritual refinement, and dyed it with a divine dye, and made it shine and clarified its essence and made it transparent."

The soul in question is a particular one. Not some rarefied, separate faculty, but the sensory soul, the nafs hissi — the very part of him that sees and hears and feels its way through the world of bodies. Every person has one, and so does the مُكَثِّر. Yet the two are not the same soul. The ordinary person and the مُكَثِّر both carry a sensory soul, but the Mukathir's has been worked upon. It has been made fine.

The road made it so. He did not reach the summit in a single leap. He passed through the ten stations of the Mustajib, the one who first answers the call; then through the ten stations of the Mumin, the one who believes and is built up; and then through the degrees of the مُكَثِّر himself, however far he climbed. A soul does not pass through all of that unmarked. A long enough road enters whoever walks it, and from all of it his soul took on a subtlety it did not have at the start.

Then — and only then, onto a soul already made subtle — something connected. The divine sciences, the ulum ilahiyya, and the spiritual secrets, the asrar malakutiyya. These did not merely inform him; they finished him. They perfected the soul with a total purity, refined it with a spiritual refinement, dyed it through with a divine dye, and left it shining, clarified, transparent. He became, in effect, a man carrying a holy spirit — his sensory soul itself transmuted into something it was not born as.

A question follows. If a refined soul is the signature of the مُكَثِّر, does it follow that any soul which seems refined belongs to a مُكَثِّر? It does not, because a person's stations are hidden, known to God alone. Outwardly a man may look like a مُكَثِّر, and his soul may genuinely be refined, and still the formal designation is not one that any person may award. That naming belongs to God.

This does not dissolve into a fog where nothing can be said. The matter resolves from the side of justice. Justice demands this: if a soul has truly become pure, then that person has in fact become a مُكَثِّر. He will have passed the ten stations of the Mumin and reached the station of the مُكَثِّر, and his soul's subtlety is the consequence of that ascent, not an accident of temperament. The subtlety need not be on display. The public title need never be conferred; the station rests with God. But where the purity of the soul is real, the rank is real — even if it is concealed from everyone but the One who made it so.

There is a precise and dangerous sense in which a higher rank becomes a god for the one beneath him, and that very danger, handled rightly, becomes the ladder of true Tawhid. The word "god" carries a sense here that is earned rather than assumed.

> فَإِذَا قَابَلَهُ الْمُسْتَفِيدُ بِالصِّدْقِ وَصِحَّةِ النِّيَّةِ وَصَفَاءِ الطَّبِيعَةِ وَتَكَلَّمَ مَعَهُ وَأَفَادَهُ مِنَ الْكَلَامِ الْمَلَكُوتِيِّ وَالْعِلْمِ الْإِلَهِيِّ الَّذِي لَمْ يَكُنْ قَدْ خَطَرَ قَبْلَ ذَلِكَ بِبَالِهِ وَلَا ظُنَّ بِمَسَامِعِهِ قَطُّ وَلَا مَسَامِعِ أَمْثَالِهِ، حَارَ فِيهِ لُبُّهُ وَوَلَهَ، فَصَارَ لَهُ إِلَهًا مَالِكًا لِرِقِّهِ عَارِفًا بِدَلَالَتِهِ وَعَظِيمِ سَبْقَتِهِ
>
> "So when the seeker receives him with sincerity and soundness of intention and purity of nature, and speaks with him, and the Mukathir bestows upon him of the spiritual speech and the divine knowledge which had never before crossed his heart nor ever been suspected by his hearing or the hearing of his likes — his intellect is bewildered in it, and he is astounded, and the Mukathir becomes for him a god, a master of his neck, knowing of his guidance and his great precedence."

The scene is a room. A seeker comes — a mustafid, one who wants to receive — and he comes the only way that works: with sincerity, with soundness of intention, with a nature unclouded. He sits. He converses. The مُكَثِّر begins to give him the spiritual speech, al-kalam al-malakuti, and the divine knowledge — knowledge so high it had never once crossed the seeker's heart. Not knowledge he had forgotten, but knowledge his ears had never suspected was there to hear, and not his ears alone: the ears of everyone like him. He had no category for it.

When a mind meets something it has no shelf to put it on, it reels. The seeker's intellect — his lubb, the kernel of his understanding — is bewildered: hara. He is astounded: walaha. He cannot work out how this man came by such a station, how such matters could live inside a human being. In that bewilderment, the مُكَثِّر becomes for him a god — an ilah, a master of his neck, malik li-riqqihi — and he recognizes the man's guidance and his great precedence on the road.

In what sense is the مُكَثِّر a "god"? It is the second of the two meanings of ilah. He is a god in the sense that he is the center of the circle. The image is a compass drawing a circle: the point in the middle does not move, and everything else moves only because the middle holds it in orbit. The disciple, dizzy with astonishment, begins to revolve around his teacher exactly as a circle revolves around its center. That revolving is his bewilderment; it has motion to it. In this sense alone — as the still point around which the staggered seeker circles — the مُكَثِّر is his "god."

It is emphatically not the other sense. He is not a creator of beings. The power to originate, the power of ibda (إبداع), was stripped from every one of the ranks at the very beginning; none of them makes anything from nothing. He is "god" only as the center of a bewildered orbit, and as the master who has hold of the seeker's neck — not to keep it, but to release it — the one whose guidance and greatness and precedence the seeker has come, truly, to recognize.

The seeker is now in orbit. But orbit is not the destination; it is the start of the lift. The bewilderment that made the teacher a "god" becomes the very engine that dethrones him.

> فَإِذَا تَحَقَّقَ افْتِقَارَهُ إِلَى مَنْ فَوْقَهُ مِنَ الْحُدُودِ وَحَاجَتَهُ إِلَيْهِ وَافْتِقَارَ الَّذِي فَوْقَهُ... مُتَنَاهِيًا ذَلِكَ إِلَى الْإِمَامِ... وَمِنْهُ إِلَى مَنْ فَوْقَهُ مِنَ الْعُقُولِ الْمُجَرَّدَاتِ مُتَنَاهِيًا ذَلِكَ
>
> "And when he verifies the Mukathir's need for the one above him among the ranks, and his poverty toward him, and the need of the one above him in turn... ending in that at the Imam... and from him toward the one above him among the abstract intellects, ending in that."

The believing seeker, the mumin, comes to verify something he could not see while he was merely dazzled: the very man before whom he stands bewildered is himself bewildered before the rank above him. The seeker sees that he is poor toward the مُكَثِّر — and that the مُكَثِّر, in turn, is poor, needy, bewildered before his own mufid, the one who pours knowledge into him. And the one above the مُكَثِّر is bewildered before the one above him. The chain does not break. Rank upon rank, the same posture repeats, all the way up through the physical ranks, the حُدُود al-jismaniyya, until it reaches the Imam, peace be upon him.

And from the Imam it does not stop. It climbs higher still, toward the abstract intellects — the uqul al-mujarradat, intellects that are not in the physical world at all, the angelic realities of the higher realms. The image is a sealed letter passing hand to hand: each bearer holds it, and each hands it on, and not one of them is the writer. The ascent runs up through these bearers until, at the very summit of the abstract intellects, it reaches the First Intellect — the Aql al-Awwal — which was itself bewildered before all the things originated and created: bewildered at how it came by its own precedence, when all of them were brought into being together, at one stroke, at one time.

> ثُمَّ تَحَقَّقَ وَلَهَهُ فِي مُبْدِعِهِ وَمُبْدِعِ أَجْنَاسِهِ وَحَيْرَتِهِ فِيهِ
>
> "Then he verifies its bewilderment at its Originator, and at the Originator of its kinds, and its perplexity in Him."

And then the last verification: the seeker confirms that even the First Intellect — the highest of all — is bewildered before its Originator, the mubdi, the One who originated it and originated every kind there is, and is perplexed before Him. So now the whole chain of bewilderment lies open, from the disciple staggering before the مُكَثِّر all the way up to the First Intellect staggering before God.

The chain carries a lesson. If everyone on the ladder is bewildered, then bewilderment is not a failure but the condition of knowing. The first step in acquiring knowledge is the confession that one does not have it. A person must become, in a sense, ignorant first — must own his not-knowing — before anything can be poured in. This is why the station of bewilderment is necessary, for the دَاعِي who calls and for every seeker who answers. As the circle revolves around its center, so the seeker revolves in his perplexity, and that very revolving is the precondition of gnosis. The dizziness does not stand in the way of the knowledge; the dizziness is the door.

Having traced the bewilderment to its source, the seeker performs the act the whole ascent was for.

> نَفَى عَنْ حَدِّهِ الَّذِي هُوَ فِي أُفُقِهِ... وَأَثْبَتَهَا لِلَّهِ تَعَالَى وَتَكَبَّرَ، الَّذِي لَا إِلَهَ إِلَّا هُوَ
>
> "He negates it from his rank, which is in his horizon... and affirms it for Allah the Exalted, and proclaims His greatness — He besides whom there is no god."

He negates divinity from the rank in his own horizon — that is, from the مُكَثِّر, the one nearest him, the one who dazzled him — and from every rank above the مُكَثِّر, physical and spiritual, all the way to the end of the chain. He says, in effect: not one of these gives me my being. Each of them is himself bewildered before another above him, and the highest of them, the First Intellect, is bewildered before the Originator. The exact condition the First Intellect held toward God — that posture of perplexity — the seeker now finds copied at every level, including his own dizziness before the مُكَثِّر. And so he affirms: this مُكَثِّر, for all his greatness and the genuine majesty of his station, which I have truly recognized and do not deny, is not my god. Above him is one, and above that one another, up to the summit, and every one of them is bewildered. The truly Real is the Originator alone — mubdi-e taala. He affirms divinity for God alone and proclaims His greatness, الَّذِي لَا إِلَهَ إِلَّا هُوَ — He besides whom there is no god.

The structure is one of linked circles. The مُكَثِّر has his circle. Above him is the circle of his mufid. Above that, another circle. And these circles are linked, one fastened to the next, ascending until the final circle, which is the First Intellect's. The believer's whole path of Tawhid runs along this linkage. First he confesses that the مُكَثِّر has become a god for him — meaning the center of his bewildered orbit. Then he verifies that the مُكَثِّر is himself in orbit around another, and so denies that the مُكَثِّر is his god in the absolute sense. And so on, up the linked circles, until he reaches the true God who stands beyond them all.

How did these circles come to be linked at all? The answer lies back in the spiritual world, on the day the dawahs — the summonses — were first given there. When a call went out, those who joined it and repented with the very repentance of the one who called — tawabu bi-tawbatihi — rose with him; they went up with him. Those who did not join were given the call again, fresh. The pattern is exact. A circle has at its center a forerunner, a sabiq. He calls. Those who answer and repent with his repentance ascend alongside him. And the last individual left behind, the one who has not risen, is handed the command: Our work is finished; now you do the work. And with that, he becomes the center of a new circle. Others gather around him and repent with his repentance, and again the last one left is handed the command in his turn.

That is how circle was generated from circle. The circle of the first person, then the circle of the Imam, then of the Bab, then of the Hujjat, and onward — each cast in the mold of the first. The pattern was set there, in the spiritual world, and every circle that came after was struck from it: the circle of the ashir, of Adam the summoner, of the Qaims, of the Dais, the Hujjats, the Imams, the circle of ain, the circle of mim — one after another, all on the one original die. And the bewilderment that orders each circle is just this: the center of any given circle, around whom others revolve, must himself revolve around the center of the circle above his own. He too is in orbit. The structure of bewildered revolution copies itself, top to bottom, the way a building's load-bearing walls decide the shape of every floor above them. As the caller says, in effect, to the one he commands: you were formed by seeing us; now go and correct those below you. And all of this — every turn of it — is folded inside the single sentence, لَآ إِلَهَ إِلَّا ٱللَّهُ.

A striking reading of the word *ilah* itself follows. The three conditions present in every one of these circles are written into the three letters of the word. Ilah — إله — is alif, lam, ha. The **alif** shows precedence without an inspirer — sabqat without a mulhim: this is the First Intellect, the Aql al-Awwal, who outstripped all the rest by his own act, with no one above him to prompt or inspire him. The **lam** shows the condition of the second, one who advances not by his own independent precedence but by seeing another and repenting with his repentance — tawabu bi-tawbatihi: the station of the one emanated from the First, the munbaith min al-awwal, who reached his rank the way the second emanation reaches its rank, by following. The **ha** shows the third condition: the giving of the dawah, which was carried out by the seven intellects, the seven uqul — for the ashir, the tenth, did not give it. These three conditions — alif and lam and ha — are present in every single circle, because in every circle there is the whole. The entire story of the life of the universe is packed into this one composition. The station of the alif is the First Intellect; the station of the lam is the one emanated from the First; and the ha is the call given by the seven. So the very letters of "god" trace out the structure — forerunner, follower, summons — that builds every circle in the hierarchy.

The act of affirmation is not yet finished. The seeker has named the true God; now he must say precisely what makes the false "gods" false.

> وَأَثْبَتَهَا لِلَّهِ تَعَالَى وَتَكَبَّرَ، الَّذِي لَا إِلَهَ إِلَّا هُوَ مِنْ هَذِهِ الْآلِهَةِ الْمَخْلُوقَةِ وَالْمُخْتَرَعَةِ وَالْمُبْتَدَعَةِ، الشَّامِلِ لِكُلِّ وَاحِدٍ مِنْهُمُ اسْمُ الْمُرَبِّي الَّذِي فَوْقَهُ وَالْحَاجَةُ الدَّاعِيَةُ لَهُ إِلَيْهِ
>
> "And he affirmed it for Allah the Exalted and proclaimed His greatness — He besides whom there is no god from among these created, invented, and originated deities, each one of whom carries the name of the nourisher who is above him and the need that calls him toward him."

He affirms divinity for God and declares: there is no god from among these "deities" — these gods that are created, makhluqa; invented, mukhtaraa; originated, mubtadaa. And here is their telltale mark, the thing that gives every false god away. Each one carries inside himself the name of the nourisher above him — the murabbi — and the need that pulls him upward toward that nourisher. That is how a created god shows itself to be created: it is sustained by one above it, and driven by a hunger toward one above it. It is never self-sufficient. A thing that needs is a thing that was made.

> إِلَّا مَنْ تَوَهَّمَتْ حَيْرَةُ عَالِيهِ وَدَانِيهِ عَلَى عُلُوِّ حَالَتِهِ

The only one who is *not* such a created god — the one with no nourisher above him and no upward-pulling need — is the one before whom the bewilderment of high and low alike is occasioned by the sheer loftiness of His state. Above Him there is nothing higher. Every subordinate is bewildered before Him; He is bewildered before none. And so:

> فَلَا إِلَهَ سِوَاهُ، لَيْسَ ذَلِكَ جَبْرِيَّةً مِنْهُمْ، لَا يَجِدُ عَنْهَا مَحِيصًا
>
> "So there is no god besides Him. It is not a compulsion upon them; he finds no escape from it."

There is no god besides that one Being. And the seeker's affirmation of Him is not a mere helpless reflex — and yet, in a way, it *is* forced: the helpless servant finds no escape, no muhas, from having to address Him *somehow.* He cannot not name Him. But the affirmation of His sole divinity is not therefore empty compulsion; it is the truth the entire ascent has just demonstrated, step by step, circle by circle.

The threefold movement completes itself at the highest level. First, transcendence:

> ثُمَّ نَزَّهَهُ تَعَالَى وَتَكَبَّرَ عَنِ الْحُدُودِ الْجِسْمَانِيَّةِ الْمَحْدُودَةِ وَعَنِ الْحُدُودِ الرُّوحَانِيَّةِ غَيْرِ الْمَحْدُودَةِ
>
> "Then he declared Him transcendent and proclaimed His greatness above the limited physical ranks and above the unlimited spiritual ranks."

This is تَنْزِيه in full. The seeker declares the one God transcendent above the physical ranks, which are limited, mahduda, and above the spiritual ranks, which are unlimited, ghayr mahduda — because the true God, the nourisher of all, is beyond *both* hierarchies, the bounded corporeal one and the unbounded spiritual one alike. Then comes the stripping, تَجْرِيد:

> ثُمَّ سَلَبَهُ تَعَالَى مَا أَثْبَتَهُ لَهُمْ مِنَ الْأَسْمَاءِ وَالصِّفَاتِ وَالنُّعُوتِ وَالْإِضَافَاتِ
>
> "Then he stripped from Him the names and attributes and descriptions and relations that he had affirmed for them."

He strips from the Originator, mubdi-e taala, all the names, attributes, descriptions — the nuut — and relations — the idafat — that he had affirmed for the ranks. Those names and attributes belong to the physical and spiritual ranks. The Originator is beyond them, for He is God in the absolute sense, divested of everything that can be predicated of anything. And finally, the return:

> وَعَادَ إِلَى حَدِّهِ وَوَلَهِهِ فِيهِ وَطَاعَتِهِ
>
> "And he returns to his own rank, and to his bewilderment in it, and to his obedience."

After the whole sweep of affirming and negating, the seeker comes *back.* The mumin is bewildered before the مُكَثِّر; above the مُكَثِّر are ranks, and ranks above those, up to the First Intellect, which is itself bewildered before another — and having traced all of it, the seeker returns and says, in effect: *each must do his own work, and I will do mine.* He comes back down to his own station, to his bewilderment within it, to his obedience and his commitment to his مُكَثِّر. And it is precisely at that moment — not on the way up, but on the way back, settled in his own place — that he becomes the one who performs true Tawhid, true تَنْزِيه, true تَجْرِيد: with gnosis, marifat; with religion, din; with knowledge, ilm; and with certainty, yaqin.

And to a soul like that, God speaks:

> يَا أَيَّتُهَا النَّفْسُ الْمُطْمَئِنَّةُ ارْجِعِي إِلَىٰ رَبِّكِ رَاضِيَةً مَّرْضِيَّةً
>
> "O tranquil soul, return to your Lord, well-pleased and well-pleasing."

The crucial word is *irjii* — *return.* The soul went all the way to the top and now comes back. That is the whole shape of it: up, and then down. "Return to your Lord" means a return to the soul's mufid, the one who bestowed upon it. And "well-pleased and well-pleasing," radiyatan mardiyya, means both at once: the soul itself content, and its mufid content with it — the pleasure running in both directions. The text unfolds the verse further:

> اطْمِئْنَانُهَا بِمَا عَرَفَتْ... وَمَرْضَاتُهَا بِأَمْرِ رَبِّهَا الَّذِي إِلَيْهِ يُرْجَعُ، مَرْضِيَّةً عِنْدَهُ... الَّذِينَ إِلَى مَعْرِفَتِهِمُ انْتَهَى وَبَلَغَ

The soul's tranquility, its itminan, lies in what it has come to *know* — its serenity is the fruit of its gnosis, not of comfort or rest. And its pleasure lies in the command of its Lord, the Lord to whom it is returned. And it is well-pleasing, mardiyya, in His sight — and in the sight of every rank whose gnosis the soul reached and arrived at along the way. And the author closes this movement on his knees:

> الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ الَّذِي هَدَانَا لِهَٰذَا وَمَا كُنَّا لِنَهْتَدِيَ لَوْلَا أَنْ هَدَانَا اللَّهُ ۖ لَقَدْ جَاءَتْ رُسُلُ رَبِّنَا بِالْحَقِّ
>
> "And praise be to Allah who guided us to this; we would not have been guided had Allah not guided us. Indeed the messengers of our Lord came with the truth."

The tranquil soul, having reached the end of the gnosis of its mufid, is called home to its Lord, pleased and pleasing both; and the praise belongs to God, who guided to this gnosis a soul that could never have found the way on its own, and whose messengers came carrying the truth.

A question naturally arises: whether any of this is in the Book. This Originator who created; this whole world of souls; the linked circles and the ascent and the return — is there any mention of it in the Quran that is recited, in the verses, in the supplications that are made? There is. The matter is conveyed in different phrases in different places — as in the verse that speaks of creation مِّن نَّفْسٍ وَاحِدَةٍ, from a single soul. But the *summary* of everything the Quran teaches about the Originator is Surah al-Fatiha — Surah al-Hamd. And its details, as Sayyidna has explained, all stand on the opening verse:

> الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ رَبِّ الْعَالَمِينَ
>
> "Praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds."

For He is Rabb al-Alamin, the Lord of all the worlds, and the qualities of God unfold out of this one verse. Every detail is built upon it — the full working stands in Kitab al-Alim wa al-Ghulam, the Book of the Master and the Disciple; whoever reads it will understand. So the matter is there, in supplication and in the Quran alike, its summary held in al-Fatiha, within which the duat have unpacked the whole teaching.

And the Fatiha holds more — it holds the three kinds of people. The دَاعِي teaches that God made three classes: the repentant, then those who incur wrath, then the astray. They stand in the verse:

> اهْدِنَا الصِّرَاطَ الْمُسْتَقِيمَ ۝ صِرَاطَ الَّذِينَ أَنْعَمْتَ عَلَيْهِمْ
>
> "Guide us upon the straight path, the path of those upon whom You have bestowed favor."

Those upon whom favor was bestowed, anamta alayhim, are the nadimin, the repentant — and the favor given them was precisely that they were granted to *return.* Then the verse turns:

> غَيْرِ الْمَغْضُوبِ عَلَيْهِمْ
>
> "not of those upon whom is wrath."

And who are the maghdub, those wrath has fallen on? The insistent ones — the musirrin — who dig in and persist in their error, and so the wrath comes down on them. And the third:

> وَلَا الضَّالِّينَ
>
> "nor of the astray."

These are the bewildered, the mutahayyirin — the ones lost in perplexity who never found their way through it. So the sirat, the path that has to be crossed, is laid before three classes: the nadimin, favored to return; the musirrin, who earn wrath by their insistence; and the mutahayyirin, who go astray in a bewilderment that never resolved. The Originator's making of beings, and the details of that making in the world of the physical body, have come down in His pure speech, revealed to the people of the world.

But there is one thing the Quran gives that is not an answer at all — it is a wall. The reality of the Originator Himself cannot be grasped, and the Book says so:

> سُبْحَانَ الَّذِي... سُبْحَانَ اللَّهِ عَمَّا يَصِفُونَ
>
> "Glory be to Him... Glory be to Allah, above what they describe."

God is pure above whatever attributes are pinned on Him; His reality cannot be understood; He Himself cannot be comprehended. This stands in many places in the Quran, and from it the conclusion is proven: the reality of God cannot be reached. *Amma yasifun* — above what they describe — means that whatever attribute is set down for Him, He is pure of it, beyond it, clear of it. This is the very meaning of تَنْزِيه: that whatever the bewildered seekers ascribe to Him — bewildered precisely *because* they cannot reach His full gnosis — He transcends it. And this incapacity does not stop short of the top. Even the First Intellect, their own mufid, the highest of the made things, was incapable of the gnosis of the Originator. *Ajiz.* The First Intellect did not possess the gnosis of mubdi-e taala; it stood bewildered before Him — and it was *on account of that very bewilderment* that the First Intellect became a god for those below it.

So what word did they finally settle on for the Originator, when no description would hold? One word. **Hu.** *He.* And even that under compulsion, because they had nothing else — no other word that would not falsely draw a circle around Him. The naming itself is a *zanbun mashfuun bil-istighfar*, a sin coupled with its own plea for forgiveness, uttered only out of necessity. For to prove one's own existence one is forced to affirm the existence of the Existent; and to affirm Him one is forced to call Him *something*; and the only word that does not lie about Him by hemming Him in is *Hu* — He.

So the seeker has done the full circuit. He climbed from his own dizziness before the teacher up through every linked circle to the First Intellect, found even that summit dizzy before God, named God by the one word that does not cage Him, and came back down to his own rank to do his own work. He knows now what a "god" is and what it is not — center of an orbit, never the maker of being. He has the structure whole. But knowing the structure of the worlds is not the same as standing inside the next of its ranks and feeling its particular weight. The first of the spiritual ranks has been named, and a soul has been watched crossing into it. The road does not stop at the naming. It runs on, into that rank itself — and it can be followed only by the road already laid: through the broken self, up the circles, and back.

chapters.chapter_key: out of nothing, and equal in justice
chapters.before_md:
The promised road runs on, and now it turns back behind the ranks themselves to ask after the act that made them. Before there was a first of the spiritual ranks for a soul to cross into, before there was any rank at all, there was an origination — a bringing-into-being out of which the ranks, the worlds, and the souls of all people came. That act is where the road turns now, drawing on a long exposition by Sayyidna Mohyuddin, whose argument follows here in summary, its bones kept whole — beginning where he begins, with the Name and then with the ground:

> إِنَّ اللَّهَ تَعَالَى الَّذِي لَا تَتَجَاسَرُ نَحْوَهُ الْخَوَاطِرُ وَلَا تَسْمُو إِلَيْهِ الْأَوْهَامُ وَالضَّمَائِرُ، أَبْدَعَ عَالَمَ الْإِبْدَاعِ الْمُكَنَّى عَنْهُ بِعَالَمِ الْأَمْرِ وَعَالَمِ الْعَقْلِ وَعَالَمِ الْقُدْسِ وَعَالَمِ الصَّفَاءِ وَعَالَمِ اللَّطَافَةِ وَبِالْعَالَمِ الرُّوحَانِيِّ دَفْعَةً وَاحِدَةً مِنْ غَيْرِ شَيْءٍ تَقَدَّمَهُمْ فَيَكُونَ لَهُمْ هَيُولَى أُولَى وَلَا مَعَ شَيْءٍ صَاحَبَهُمْ فَيَكُونَ مُمَاثِلًا لَهُمْ وَمُشَاكِلًا وَلَا عَلَى شَيْءٍ أَقَلَّهُمْ فَيَكُونَ لَهُمْ مَكَانًا أَوَّلًا.
>
> "Indeed Allah the Exalted, toward whom the passing thoughts dare not turn, and toward whom imaginations and the inmost selves cannot rise, originated the world of origination — which is alluded to as the world of command, the world of intellect, the world of sanctity, the world of purity, the world of subtlety, and the spiritual world — in a single instant: not from any thing preceding them that would be a prior matter for them, nor with any thing accompanying them that would be similar and like to them, nor upon any thing bearing them that would be a first place for them."

The first clause deserves weight before the rest. He is a Being toward whom the passing thoughts — the *khawatir*, the fleeting motions that cross a mind unbidden — dare not even turn. And the imaginations, the *awham* (أوهام), together with the *zamair*, the inmost folds of the self where a person is most privately himself, cannot rise toward Him, cannot grow lofty enough to reach Him. The attempt shows what happens: a thought sets out and falls back; the inmost self reaches up and sinks down. Neither the outward instrument nor the secret one can climb to Him. That is the One in question — and it is this One who originated the world of origination, the *alam al-ibda* (عالم الإبداع).

This one originated realm wears a cluster of names. He calls it the world of command, the world of intellect, the world of sanctity, the world of purity, the world of subtlety, and the spiritual world — six titles laid beside the name *alam al-ibda* itself, seven names in all for a single thing. The crowd of names is not seven realms. There is one realm here, seen from seven sides.

One word governs everything that follows: *ibda* (إبداع), origination, which is not the same as *khalq*, creation. Ordinary speech uses both loosely, but here they part ways sharply. *Khalq*, creation, is what happens when what already exists is rearranged. A thing already present is broken, reshaped, recombined, and a new composite form is brought out of it — the form is altered, but a matter is presupposed underneath. The potter creates the jar, yet the clay was waiting in his hands. That is *khalq*: form changed upon matter already given. *Ibda* is something else entirely. *Ibda* is origination from nothing, where no prior thing exists at all — no clay, no hands worth of waiting stuff, nothing. And the world in question is created by *ibda* in exactly this strict sense.

That is why Mohyuddin does not merely assert it but seals it with three denials, each meant to land. First: it was originated *not from any thing that preceded it*. There was no prior substance lying ready to serve as its *hayula* — its prime matter, the first leaven a baker folds his dough from. Second: it was originated *not with any accompanying thing*. There was no co-present matter standing alongside it, nothing it could be shaped to match, nothing it could resemble or take after. Third: it was originated *not upon any thing bearing it*. There was no underlying floor, no substrate to be its *makan* (اَلْمَكَان), its first place, the location a thing rests upon. No matter before it, no matter beside it, no place beneath it. With all three stripped away, what is left is *ibda* in its purity: the world of origination brought forth in a single instant — *dafatan wahidatan* — out of nothing whatsoever.

Here a question arises that cannot be set aside. If He needed nothing and used nothing, why originate at all? Mohyuddin gives the answer plainly:

> وَاخْتَرَعَهُمْ عَالَمًا، وُجُودًا مِنْ عَدَمٍ غَيْرِ مَوْجُودٍ، تَفَضُّلًا مِنْهُ وَجُودًا وَتَطَوُّلًا مِنْهُ.
>
> "And He originated them as a world — existence from a non-existent nothingness — as a favor from Him, and generosity, and bestowal from Him."

He originated the existents — *ikhtaraa* — and drew them up into a world of existence, pulling them out of an *adam* (آدَم), a nothingness, that was not itself existent. Against this a picture must be guarded, one the mind will try to paint. *Adam* is not some shadowy realm, a dim warehouse of the not-yet-made. It is no realm and no place. It is simply the absence of being — the bare fact that a thing is not. A teacher in Sindh once turned to his students and asked them: when all this was taking place, where were *we*? The question is the whole lesson. There was no "where." There was nothing but non-existence, and it is out of that nothing that all things were drawn. The warehouse falls away: before being, there is no place anything was waiting in; there is only the not.

And the cause of it all was not need and not compulsion but pure favor. *Tafaddulan minhu* — a favor from Him. *Wa judan* — and generosity, a free gift. *Wa tatawwulan minhu* — and a bestowal, an unowed boon. On this single point — why the Originator originated — Mohyuddin does not write a line and move on. He writes chapter after chapter, and what he does in them is patient and almost relentless: he takes up every supposed purpose, every conceivable need or motive one might attribute to the act, and he negates it, one after another, refusing each in turn, until only one thing is left standing. The favor itself was the only "purpose." He originated out of sheer favor, generosity, and bestowal, and out of nothing besides. He grounds it like this:

> إِذْ مِنْ شِيمَةِ الْكَرِيمِ الْقَادِرِ التَّفَضُّلُ، وَمِنْ سَجِيَّةِ الْعَزِيزِ الْعَظِيمِ الْجُودُ، لَا مُحْتَاجًا إِلَيْهِمْ وَلَا عَابِثًا بِهِمْ، إِذْ هُوَ مُتَعَالٍ مُتَكَبِّرٌ عَنْ ذَلِكَ.
>
> "Since it is of the nature of the Generous, the Powerful, to bestow favor, and of the nature of the Mighty, the Great, to be generous — not needing them nor playing with them, since He is exalted and transcendent above that."

It belongs to the very *shimah*, the ingrained nature, of the Generous and the Powerful to bestow favor; it belongs to the very *sajiyyah*, the inborn disposition, of the Mighty and the Great to give and to give freely. So He brought the existents into being — and here two errors fall away together. Not because He needed them: the Giver had no need of the given, none at all. And not as idle sport: He was not amusing Himself with them, not making them to pass an eternity, for He is exalted and transcendent far above any such thing. The origination simply flowed from the bestowing nature of the Generous and Mighty, with no need driving it and no frivolity staining it.

What remains is *how* the originated beings came forth — in what shape, of what stature. He says:

> أَوْجَدَهُمْ أَشْبَاحًا صُورِيَّةً مَحْضَةً نُورَانِيَّةً، ذَوَاتِ قَامَةٍ أَلْفِيَّةٍ كَالْقَامَةِ الْإِنْسَانِيَّةِ الْبَشَرِيَّةِ، مُبَايِنَةً لِأَنْفُسِهِمُ الْهَيُولَانِيَّةِ.
>
> "He brought them into existence as forms, purely imaginal and luminous, possessing thousand-fold statures like the human, corporeal statures, distinct from their material souls."

He brought them into existence as *ashbah* — forms — and these forms were purely imaginal, *suriyyah*; pure, *mahdah*; and luminous, *nuraniyya*. They stood at statures of a thousand-fold measure, *qamat alfiyya*, likened to the human bodily stature, *al-qamat al-insaniyya al-bashariyya*. The direction of the comparison needs setting straight, or it reads exactly backward. The originated forms are called *like* the human stature — but that is said only to make the matter graspable to people, who know the human shape and nothing higher. In reality the likeness runs the other way. The human stature is patterned upon those originated forms; they are not patterned upon it. When the Originator originated, He originated in such a way that the human bodies which would much later enter the world were fashioned on the model of those primordial luminous forms. So although the words say the forms resembled the human stature, the truth is that the human stature was cut to the model of the forms. The copy reaches up to describe the original by pointing at the copy.

And these luminous forms are *distinct* — *mubayinah* — from the material souls, the *anfus hayulaniyya*, that came afterward. The souls did not yet exist; they belong to a later stage. The order here is a descent. What was originated were luminous imaginal forms, *ashbah suriyyah nuraniyya*. When souls were later formed, they were a fallen, degraded condition drawn down from these. And when bodies of flesh and blood were formed, they were a condition more fallen still. The forms were luminous subtleties — *lataif nuraniyya*. The bodies are dark densities — *kathaif zulmaniyya*. The soul is a fallen form of the luminous original; the body, a yet more fallen form of that. One light at the top, and as it descends it thickens and darkens, like clear water that grows muddied as it sinks to the riverbed.

The first of the perfections follows, a doctrine that carries weight, for it is the seedbed of justice itself:

> فَأَوْجَدَ تِلْكَ الْأَشْبَاحَ النُّورَانِيَّةَ مُتَسَاوِيَةً فِي الْكَمَالِ الْأَوَّلِيِّ الَّذِي هُوَ الْوُجُودُ وَالْحَيَاةُ وَالْقُوَّةُ وَالْقُدْرَةُ، لَا تَخَالُفَ فِيهَا وَلَا تَفَاضُلَ وَلَا تَبَايُنَ بَيْنَهَا وَلَا تَمَايُلَ فِيمَا دَقَّ وَجَلَّ وَكَثُرَ وَقَلَّ، عَدْلًا مِنْهُ عَزَّ وَجَلَّ.
>
> "So He brought those luminous forms into existence, equal in the first perfection — which is existence, life, strength, and ability — with no disagreement in them, no preference, no distinction among them, and no inclination in what was subtle or great, much or little, as an act of justice from Him, the Mighty and Majestic."

He brought the luminous forms into existence *equal* — *mutasawiyah* — in the first perfection, the *kamal al-awwali*. And what is this first perfection? It is the original state in which He made them, and it is made of four things: existence, *wujud*; life, *hayat*; strength, *quwwah*; and ability — which, with Mohyuddin, means knowledge and power together, *ilm* and *qudrah*. In that first perfection the forms were equal, equal with no gap of any kind. No disagreement among them, *la takhaluf*. No preference of one over another, *la tafadul*. No distinction, *la tabayun*. No leaning of one above the rest, *la tamayul* — not in the subtle, not in the great, not in the much, not in the little. The first He originated was exactly as the last He originated. Not a hair's difference ran between any of the originated beings in the state of first perfection.

And this equality was no accident of the making. It was an act of *adl*, of justice, from Him, mighty and majestic. He grounds the principle:

> إِذِ الْعَادِلُ يَتَسَاوَى عَدْلُهُ وَالْفَاضِلُ يَعُمُّ فَضْلُهُ.
>
> "Since the justice of the Just is equal, and the grace of the Gracious is universal."

The justice of the Just is even in its distribution — it does not parcel out more here and less there. The grace of the Gracious is universal in its reach — it does not water one field and leave the next dry. Therefore the originated forms came into being in perfect equality. That is not a sentiment; it is a conclusion drawn from who the Maker is. And it is anchored, finally, in scripture itself:

> كَمَا أَخْبَرَ الْكِتَابُ الْكَرِيمُ مِنْ قَوْلِ الْعَلِيِّ الْعَظِيمِ: ﴿وَلَوْ كَانَ مِنْ عِنْدِ غَيْرِ اللَّهِ لَوَجَدُوا فِيهِ اخْتِلَافًا كَثِيرًا﴾
>
> "As the Noble Book has informed, from the saying of the High, the Great: And if it had been from other than Allah, they would have found in it much contradiction."

Had this originated order proceeded from any maker other than Allah, much contradiction — *ikhtilaf* — would be found woven through it; for only a perfect justice could bring forth a creation without disparity. The word *ikhtilaf* itself is worth weighing. It comes from the root *khalf* and arrives in the pattern of *bab al-iftial*; its plain sense is difference, discrepancy, things failing to agree. The verse declares that, had the matter come from other than Allah, such discrepancy would be found running all through it. But it came from Allah, and so He showed His creation this one great kindness — He gave to none of them more and to none of them less. What He gave, He gave evenly. This is the very verse that answers the question raised earlier, whether the equal creation of all beings has any warrant in the Holy Quran. It has its warrant here, in *wa law kana min indi ghayrillahi la-wajadu fihi ikhtilafan kathira*. The equality is not a borrowed philosophy. It is in the Book.

The same reality is affirmed by Sayyidna Hamiduddin — may Allah sanctify his soul — in the seventh path, the *mashra*, of the fourth form, the *suwar*, of his *Rahat al-Aql*. His words carry the matter forward, for they answer a question the simultaneity raised some pages earlier: how could a whole world come into being all at once?

> وَدَارُ الْإِبْدَاعِ وَالِانْبِعَاثِ لَا عَائِقَ فِيهَا لِخُلُوِّهِمَا مِنَ الْمَوَادِّ الَّتِي تَعُوقُ وَتَجَرُّدِهَا مِنْهَا وَكَوْنِهَا صُوَرًا مَحْضَةً لَا تَتَعَلَّقُ بِمَادَّةٍ وَلَا بِهَا مَادَّةٌ لِتَحْجُزَهَا عَنِ الْفِعْلِ.
>
> "And in the abode of origination and the abode of emanation there is no obstacle, because of their freedom from the matters that obstruct, and their being abstracted from them, and their being pure forms attached to no matter, with no matter in them that would prevent them from action."

In the abode of origination, *dar al-ibda*, and the abode of emanation, *dar al-inbiath*, there is no obstacle — *la aiqa*. And why none? Because both abodes are *free* of the obstructing matters; the kinds of stuff that would impede are simply not there. The forms are abstracted, *tajarrud*, from all such matter. They are pure forms, *suwar mahdah*, clinging to no matter, with no matter clinging in them. Matter is the thing that obstructs. Wherever matter sits, hindrance and friction arise — the way a current slows the instant it meets silt and stone. But here there is no matter at all to halt the forms from *fil*, from action. There is power present, *quwwah*; there is ability present, *qudrah*; and they can show their effect with nothing standing in their way. No drag has been set across them to delay the second action or to block the reaching of the second perfection. And from this Hamiduddin draws the conclusion the whole passage was built toward:

> وَإِذَا كَانَ لَا عَائِقَ فِيهَا فَوُجُودُ مَوْجُودَاتِهَا لَا بِزَمَانٍ بَلْ دَفْعَةً وَاحِدَةً، مِثْلَ وُجُودِ إِشْرَاقِ بَسِيطِ الْهَوَاءِ عَنْ ضَوْءِ الشَّمْسِ، لَا بِزَمَانٍ... وَإِضَاءَةُ النَّارِ الْبَيْتَ الْمُظْلِمَ دَفْعَةً وَاحِدَةً، لَا بِزَمَانٍ.
>
> "And since there is no obstacle in them, the existence of their existents is not in time but in a single instant — like the illumination of the expanse of the air by the light of the sun, not in time... and like the lighting of a dark house by a fire in a single instant, not in time."

Because nothing obstructs, the existents of these abodes came to be not in time — *la bi-zaman* — but in a single instant, *dafatan wahidatan*, all of them at one stroke. He gives two images, both meant to do their work. The first: the sun rises, and the whole expanse of the air is flooded with light at once — not lit strip by strip, near things first and far things after, but the entire reach of it illumined in the same moment. The second: a dark room, and a flame is kindled in it; the instant the fire catches, the whole room is full of light. Not a slow filling from the lamp outward, but the room itself, in one moment, bright. So too the world of origination came into existence — like air all at once awash in sunlight, like a dark house all at once illumined.

That simultaneity carries a consequence, drawn out in the line that follows:

> عَلَى أَنَّ الشَّيْءَ فِي تِلْكَ الدَّارِ لَمْ يَتَقَدَّمْ وُجُودُهُ عَلَى شَيْءٍ مِنَ الْعُقُولِ الْقَائِمَةِ بِالْفِعْلِ وَالْعُقُولِ الْقَائِمَةِ بِالْقُوَّةِ، بَلْ وُجُودُ الْكُلِّ مَعًا.
>
> "That a thing in that abode — its existence did not precede anything of the intellects existing in actuality and the intellects existing in potentiality. Rather, the existence of all was together."

In that abode no thing's existence came before another's. The existence of the intellects subsisting *in actuality*, *bi-l-fil*, did not arrive ahead of the intellects subsisting *in potentiality*, *bi-l-quwwah*. And what are the intellects "in potentiality"? They are, in effect, the powers granted to the intellects — powers that were afterward actualized and made firm. Their existence was not preceded by some earlier existing thing; rather, the existence of all was together, *wujud al-kull maan*, at one and the same time. The intellect subsisting potentially and the intellect subsisting actually both stood in being from the same instant. And this carries a momentous result: there was no interval of time dividing the first perfection, *kamal al-awwal*, from the second perfection, *kamal al-thani*. No span of time stood between them. The potential and the actual coexisted from the very outset, so that no temporal gap was wedged between the initial state of equality and the higher state still to be attained.

One point must be conceded honestly. Human understanding needs *some* stretch of time to walk through this. Even the kindling of a fire seems, to the mind, to take a moment before the room brims with light — first the flame, then the spreading, then the brightness. But the light in question is not ordinary light that travels and spreads by degrees. It is such that the very instant it is lit, the whole is full at once. That instantaneity is the character of the first perfection itself.

Yet equality is not the same as safety. With Mohyuddin, what the first perfection does and does not include must be stated exactly:

> يُرِيدُ بِذَلِكَ أَعْلَى اللَّهُ قُدْسَهُ فِي حَالِ وُجُودِهِمُ الْأَوَّلِ وَكَمَالِهِمُ الْأَوَّلِ الَّذِينَ هُمْ فِيهِ مُتَسَاوُونَ، كَمَا سَبَقَ مِنْ قَوْلِهِ، وَهُمْ مَعَ ذَلِكَ فِي بَدْءِ وُجُودِهِمُ الْجَمِيعِ فِي الْفِعْلِ وَالْعَمَلِ غَيْرُ مَعْصُومِينَ مِنَ الْخَطَأِ.
>
> "By that — may Allah sanctify his soul — he means: in the state of their first existence and their first perfection, in which they are all equal, as has preceded from his saying; and yet, along with that, in the beginning of their collective existence, in action and deed, they are not infallible from error."

By this he means the state of the beings' first existence and first perfection — the state in which they are all equal. A qualification changes everything: along with that equality, in the beginning of their collective existence, in *fil* and عَمَل, in action and deed, they are *not infallible* — *ghayru masumin* — from error, from *khata*. The point overturns an easy assumption. The first perfection, for all its flawless equality, is not the perfect, protected state. The truly perfected state is the second perfection, the *kamal al-thani*. The first perfection is the lower, initial condition, and in it the beings, equal though they are, are not shielded from error; error can issue from them.

Then what is this "error"? Exactness matters here, for vagueness would betray the whole teaching. The error consists in *failing to attain the second perfection*. That is the error — and it wears more than one face. It is a delay in answering the invitation when the call comes. It is a refusal to rise when summoned. And beyond falling short oneself, it is the misleading of others, the setting of other souls onto the wrong road. All of this can come from beings who stand in the first perfection, precisely because in that state they are *ghayr masum*, not preserved. The first perfection, then, is best understood for what it truly is: a test placed in their hands, charging them to go straight and to use rightly the powers given them. It is not yet the state of the return-perfected. It is the trial-state of equality, the level ground from which each one must journey — by the right use of his own powers — up to the second perfection. Equal at the starting line, and free to run true or to stumble.

At just this point Mohyuddin lifts a prayer, and its grammar carries the meaning of "error" more precisely than any paraphrase could:

> عَصَمَنَا اللَّهُ مِنْ أَنْ نَزِلَّ أَوْ نُزِلَّ، بِحَقِّ مُحَمَّدٍ وَآلِهِ الطَّاهِرِينَ صَلَوَاتُ اللَّهِ عَلَيْهِمْ أَجْمَعِينَ.
>
> "May Allah protect us from slipping or being made to slip, by the right of Muhammad and his pure progeny, the blessings of Allah upon them all."

May Allah protect us — from what? From two things, and the difference between them is the difference of a single letter at the front of a verb. *An nazilla*: that we should slip. *Nuzilla*: that we should be made to slip — or that we should make others slip. The contrast is instructive, and the forms set side by side, as a grammarian would place them, show it. زَلَّ means "he slipped"; أَزَلَّ means "he made another slip." It runs exactly as قَطَعَ means "he cut" and أَقْطَعَ means "he had another cut," or as سَجَدَ means "he prostrated" and أَسْجَدَ means "he made another prostrate." So نَزِلَّ is "that we should slip," and نُزِلَّ is "that we should be made to slip," or "that we should make others slip." The same pattern governs going astray as well: زَلَّ, "he went astray"; أَضَلَّ, "he led another astray" — he went off the road himself, or he turned someone else off it. The rule never wavers: فَعَلَ, "he did," and أَفْعَلَ, "he had it done."

So the prayer asks for shelter from both at once — from slipping, and from being the cause of another's slip. And that is no accident of piety, for those two are exactly the two faces of the "error" just named, the error that is failure to reach the second perfection: to fall short of it oneself, or to mislead others and drag them short of it as well. To go astray, and to lead astray — the prayer covers them both because the danger comes in both. And with that prayer, the road bends again. The act of origination has been entered, a whole world watched coming up out of nothing in a single instant, all things seen set equal as a matter of justice, and the equality learned to be a beginning and not a guarantee. What remains is the ground that equality opens onto, where the test set into the first perfection begins to be met or failed.

chapters.chapter_key: the first to say there is no god but he
chapters.before_md:
One of those forms turned, and looked.

That is where it begins — not with a command from above, not with a voice breaking into the silence, but with a single originated form, standing among its equals, that turned its attention inward and looked. The letter renders it so, and the whole of the account hangs on this one motion. He looked with his own essence at his own essence, and then he lifted that same gaze and looked at the others — the children of his kind, his fellows, the whole crowd of forms that had come up out of nothing alongside him in that single instant. He saw himself. He saw them. And something occurred to him that had not occurred before.

The letter sets it down in these words:

> ثُمَّ إِنَّ وَاحِدًا مِنْ تِلْكَ الْأَشْبَاحِ الصُّورِيَّةِ نَظَرَ بِذَاتِهِ إِلَىٰ ذَاتِهِ وَإِلَىٰ أَبْنَاءِ جِنْسِهِ، فَعَلِمَ أَنَّ لَهُمْ مُبْدِعًا بِخِلَافِهِمْ، فَنَفَىٰ عَنْهُ وَعَنْ أَبْنَاءِ جِنْسِهِ الْإِلَٰهِيَّةَ وَأَثْبَتَهَا لِمُبْدِعِهِمْ تَعَالَىٰ وَشَهِدَ لَهُ بِالْوَحْدَانِيَّةِ.
>
> "Then indeed one of those imaginal forms looked, with his essence, at his essence and at the children of his kind; so he knew that they had an Originator unlike them; so he negated divinity from himself and from the children of his kind, and affirmed it for their Originator, the Exalted, and bore witness to His oneness."

The verb itself is exact. He looked with his essence — not with borrowed eyes, not with an instrument handed to him, but by means of the very being he had been given. He had nothing else to look with. And what his looking yielded was not a feeling but a knowing. He knew — and the word in the letter is exactly that, knew — that there was, for himself and for all of them, an Originator who was unlike them. Unlike them: there is the hinge. He did not find the Originator standing in the crowd as the tallest among equals. He found that the One who had brought them all into being could not be of their kind at all, because everything of their kind had been brought into being, and the One who does the bringing cannot be among the things brought.

So he did two things in one breath. He took divinity away from himself and from every form like him. He could not say, I am the god, and neither could any of his fellows, because he had just seen that all of them stood on the same side of the line — the originated side. And then, having cleared the false claim off himself and off his entire kind, he set divinity down where it belonged: he affirmed it for their Originator, the Exalted, and stood as witness to the fact that this Originator is one.

He has just performed, untaught, a complete act. He has denied any partner — that is the unity, the Tawhid. He has stripped the Creator of every likeness to the creature — that is تَنْزِيه, the keeping-pure. And he has cut the Originator free from being bound up in His creation, set apart from all of it — that is تَجْرِيد, the isolating of the One. Three movements that a whole tradition would later name and number, and he did them at once, in a single act of looking. By that act he became what the letter calls Sahib al-Tawhid — the Possessor of Tawhid, the one in whose hands the declaration of oneness first rested. The first ever to say it. By looking at his own essence and at his kind, by recognizing an Originator unlike them, by lifting divinity off everything that had been originated and laying it on the Originator alone, he enacted the whole of Tawhid in its completeness, all three branches together.

Yet seeing the truth is not the same as drawing near to it, and he knew that too. What he did next was subtler, and no less decisive.

> وَاعْتَرَفَ لَهُ بِالرُّبُوبِيَّةِ وَسَبَّحَ لَهُ وَخَشَعَ وَتَذَلَّلَ وَخَضَعَ وَتَوَسَّلَ بِعَظَمَتِهِ إِلَيْهِ وَتَضَرَّعَ.
>
> "And he acknowledged for Him Lordship, and glorified Him, and was reverent, and humbled himself, and submitted, and sought means through His greatness toward Him, and supplicated."

He acknowledged that the Originator is Lord — rububiyya, the Lordship that owns and sustains. He glorified Him. He grew reverent, lowered himself, gave himself over. And then comes the phrase the letter dwells on: he sought means through His greatness toward Him. That is tawassul, and it is more subtle than it sounds. The first form did not try to walk straight up to the Originator, because there is no walking straight up to Him; the Originator cannot be reached directly, not by a form, not by anyone. So the form did something else. He took the Originator's own greatness — that vast, unapproachable magnitude — and made that his road. He could not reach the Originator, so he reached toward the greatness, and let the greatness carry his approach. Through the means of that greatness he gave his testimony: that this is the Lord, that this is the divine, and that he himself was nothing, low, in need. He did not presume on a direct nearness that no creature can have. He made the very greatness of the Originator the go-between by which he could turn his face toward Him. This is what tawassul is — to take the greatness of the Originator as the means to the Originator, precisely because the Originator Himself is out of reach.

And the seeking of means was answered. Something came down.

> فَتَدَارَكَ مِنْ مُبْدِعِهِ الْمَوَادُّ الْإِلَٰهِيَّةُ وَالتَّأْيِيدَاتُ الْوَحْدَانِيَّةُ، وَاتَّصَلَ بِهِ الْعِلْمُ الْجَارِي وَالنُّورُ السَّارِي الَّذِي هُوَ كَلِمَةُ اللَّهِ تَعَالَىٰ.
>
> "So there reached him from his Originator the divine supports and the confirmations of oneness, and there connected with him the flowing knowledge and the spreading light, which is the Word of Allah, the Exalted."

From the Originator there reached him supports — divine reinforcements — and confirmations of the very oneness he had just witnessed, as if his testimony were being sealed from above. And then something connected with him: a flowing knowledge and a spreading light. Both words move. The knowledge flows; the light spreads. They are not a static deposit but a current, and the letter says plainly what that current is — it is the Word of Allah, the Exalted. That Word, that kalimah, is the one sentence around which this whole edifice is built:

> لَا إِلَٰهَ إِلَّا اللَّهُ
>
> "There is no god but God."

Through that first form's act — his negation, his recognition, his seeking of means — there flowed into him the flowing knowledge and the spreading light that is the kalimah, There is no god but God. The Word stands between the Originator and the originated like a channel cut between a spring and the field below it; before the water can reach the field, the channel must exist, and once it exists the water never stops. So with the kalimah: it is the link through which the knowledge and the light pour down from the One who has no likeness to the things that bear His mark. The letter adds the teaching that places it exactly:

> وَلِذَٰلِكَ قِيلَ إِنَّ الْكَلِمَةَ فَوْقَ الْعَقْلِ وَدُونَ الْمُبْدِعِ. وَتُسَمَّىٰ أَيْضًا بِالْأَمْرِ.
>
> "And for that reason it is said that the kalimah is above the intellect and below the Originator. And it is also named the command."

Above the intellect, below the Originator. The Word There is no god but God sits in precisely this middle station — beneath the Originator who has no station, and above the intellect that will receive what comes through it. The light came from the Originator, down to the Word, and through the Word to the intellect; the Word is the continuous link in which the Originator's will and the sentence There is no god but God are shown together, will and Word manifest as one thing. And the same Word carries a second name: al-amr, the command — because every command there is has been folded inside it. The Word is not a flash that fires once and goes dark. It is a link held open for as long as creation lasts. As long as the creation stands, the kalimah stands, and the light keeps flowing through it.

There is a consequence here that the letter draws out, and it explains a number that recurs. The world of origination ended at seven. The First Intellect came to be, the Originator made seven, and the tenth is the ashir — but the luminous world stopped at seven. Why seven and not more? Because the Originator willed it to be seven. He had placed everything inside the kalimah, and He willed that the whole of it should terminate at seven. The will set the boundary, and the boundary held.

Through that Word, the First Intellect came into a knowledge that left nothing out.

> وَبِهِ أَحَاطَ بِكُلِّ شَيْءٍ عِلْمًا وَعَلِمَ مَا كَانَ وَمَا سَيَكُونُ.
>
> "And through it he encompassed all things in knowledge, and knew what was and what will be."

Through the Word he encompassed every single thing in knowledge, and knew what had already been and what was still to come — because There is no god but God contains it all, everything that has happened and everything that has not yet happened. But the letter insists on a sequence easily reversed, and reversing it spoils the whole matter. The complete knowledge had, in a manner, already been handed over with the first perfection. It was there. What was missing was that the First Intellect did not recognize what he held, did not know how to use it. He was like a man given the keys to a house he does not yet know is his. What the light of the kalimah supplied was not new information so much as the understanding of what he had been given and the way to wield the powers already in his hands.

And there was a price of entry. Before he could take hold of the kalimah and its light, he had first to negate himself — to say, in effect, I am not my own maker. The same words the first form had spoken: I am not my creator; our creator is someone else. The First Intellect had to confess that he and all his kind were not their own creators, that their Creator was another. The instant he said it — the instant of self-negation — the kalimah was his, and in the light of the kalimah everything was his. The order never reverses: the self-emptying comes first, then the gift. One must own one's own not-being-the-creator before the Word and its all-encompassing light are placed in his hands. The denial of the false claim is the doorway; there is no other way in.

And once he was inside, the letter records what he found in his own essence:

> وَوَجَدَ فِي ذَاتِهِ مِنَ السُّرُورِ وَالْجَذَلِ وَالْحُبُورِ وَالْعِصْمَةِ وَالثَّنَاءِ وَالْعَظَمَةِ وَالْكِبْرِيَاءِ مَا لَا يَقْدِرُ أَنْ يَسْطُرَ صِفَتَهُ بَنَانٌ وَلَا يُتَرْجِمُ عَنْهُ لِسَانٌ.
>
> "And he found in his essence, of joy and delight and happiness and protection and praise and greatness and pride, that whose description no fingertip could write nor any tongue translate."

Joy, delight, happiness, protection, praise, greatness, pride — he found all of it inside himself, and so much of it that no fingertip could ever write its description and no tongue could ever translate its account. From the light of the Word he had come to know that beyond death there is salvation, and the knowing filled him with a gladness that runs past the end of every pen and the limit of every voice.

The letter now reads the inner make of this Word, treating the sentence There is no god but God as a blueprint of the whole of creation, built up in layers; and once the layers appear, they appear everywhere.

The simplest division comes first. The Word is a negation and an affirmation — that is two. There is no god is the denial; but God is the establishing. Two halves, the no and the yes. Descending into the word ilah itself, the word for "god," there are three letters — alif, lam, ha — that is three. Then there are what the letter calls the jewels of the letters — that is five. Then the words of the sentence counted outright — la, ilaha, illa, Allah — that is four. And after all this, the count of the one comes to rest at seven. There are also seven muqattaat, the disjoined letters at which the pen stops, or the tongue halts — and this is the same seven again. The luminous world ended at seven luminous forms for exactly this reason: because of these seven places where the pen comes to a stop. In the world of light the matter closed at seven forms, and it closed there because There is no god but God, by the will of the Originator, was meant to close at seven; He had placed everything within the Word and willed that it end at seven, and so it did. After the seven come twelve, and the twelve are the ascending spirits, the ruh-i-saidah. This same composition runs through everything — in every Imam, in every barzakh, in every believer, among all that exists: the pattern of two, three, four, seven, and twelve operates throughout, the same skeleton beneath every body. And seven and twelve together make nineteen.

Those nineteen appear in the line every act begins with:

> بِسْمِ اللَّهِ الرَّحْمَٰنِ الرَّحِيمِ
>
> "In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful."

Within it the numbers return. The two are in Bismillah and al-Rahman — in the two kinds of grammatical construction the phrase contains: the additive construction, tarkib-i-idafi, where one noun is bound to another by belonging, and the descriptive construction, tarkib-i-tawsifi, where a noun is followed by what describes it. And of these two the letter sets a rank: the additive construction is the more excellent, the descriptive the lesser. It notices, too, a strange thing about There is no god but God itself — that its order runs, as it were, upside down, for in the deeper reading the affirming comes before the denying; the reversal has come inverted, and of this it is said: Let my affirmation be established by your negation; let me be negated such that only You remain. In Bismillah al-Rahman al-Rahim the additive construction is a most exalted construction, and the descriptive lesser than it.

Here the letter brings in a master's reading — the explanation of Sayyidna Muhammad Taher, may Allah sanctify his soul, on the structure of Bismillah. Bismillah is seven letters, and those seven letters are the week of the seven Imams. With each Imam stand twelve of his deputies, his naqibs, twelve in number, and those twelve are al-Rahman al-Rahim. So the opening phrase carries the week of the seven Imams, each Imam with his Sath, his Imam, and his Madhun, the whole thing raised on the pattern of that week of seven. And the twelve naqibs are, in truth, present with every Imam. But when the seventh Imam appears, the twelve who appear alongside him are of a far higher rank than the twelve who came before — higher, because he is a mursal, one sent as a messenger. So in Muhammad Taher's reading the additive and descriptive constructions of Bismillah al-Rahman al-Rahim encode the seven Imams and their twelve naqibs, and again the additive construction stands as the more excellent of the two.

A being who had just been handed all of this — the Word, the all-encompassing knowledge, the joy past writing — might be expected to swell. He did the opposite.

> ثُمَّ ازْدَادَ لِذَٰلِكَ لِمُبْدِعِهِ تَعَالَىٰ تَذَلُّلًا وَخُضُوعًا وَحَيْرَةً فِي عَظَمَتِهِ وَخُشُوعًا.
>
> "Then, because of that, he increased toward his Originator the Exalted in humility and submission and bewilderment at His greatness and reverence."

The more he was given, the lower he bent. He grew in humility toward his Originator, in submission, in a bewilderment standing before that greatness, in reverence. The knowing did not puff him up; it pressed him down. And this is no private curiosity of his — the letter grounds it in the Book:

> وَلِذَٰلِكَ نَطَقَ الْكِتَابُ الْكَرِيمُ بِقَوْلِهِ تَعَالَىٰ: إِنَّمَا يَخْشَى اللَّهَ مِنْ عِبَادِهِ الْعُلَمَاءُ
>
> "And for that reason the Noble Book spoke with His saying, the Exalted: Indeed, only those of knowledge among His servants fear Allah."

Only the learned among His servants fear Allah. The grammar carries the weight here. The ma in innama is not, in this place, the ma that negates; it is the ma that intensifies, lending the force of indeed, the ma itself superfluous — zaidah — so that the sentence means: indeed it is only the learned among His servants who fear Him, the ma carrying the force of illa, of "except," of "none but." Every knower of the secret of creation and the causes that run through nature is, of all people, the one who fears Allah most. And this fear must not be mistaken for another. It is not dread, not the cringing away from a threat. It is the acknowledgment of His greatness. The more the knowledge increases, the more the awe deepens in the divine presence — not terror, but the recognition of a majesty too large to stand before lightly. Here stands the example of Amir al-Din al-Sadiq, peace be upon him: when the color would drain from a man's face in his presence, he would ask him, Do you not know in whose court you are standing? That is fear rightly understood — the acknowledgment of the greatness of the One before whom one stands.

And now the letter raises the First Intellect to his full station, the one toward which everything has moved.

> ثُمَّ إِنَّ اللَّهَ تَعَالَىٰ اتَّخَذَهُ لَهُ حِجَابًا وَجَعَلَهُ لَهُ بَابًا لَا يُتَوَسَّلُ إِلَيْهِ إِلَّا بِهِ وَلَا يُنَاجَىٰ إِلَّا مِنْ جَنَابِهِ وَلَا يُوَحَّدُ إِلَّا مِنْ أَسْبَابِهِ، فَصَارَ اسْمُهُ الْأَعْظَمُ وَمَقَامُهُ الْأَشْرَفُ الْأَكْرَمُ.
>
> "Then indeed Allah the Exalted took him as a veil for Himself and made him a gate for Himself, through whom alone one may seek means to Him, and from whose presence alone one may hold intimate discourse, and through whose means alone He is declared One; so he became His Greatest Name and His most noble, most honorable station."

Allah took the First Intellect as a veil for Himself and made him a gate — the one door of access to the divine. And three things were vested in that gate, three and no exceptions. There is no seeking of means to Allah except through him: the road to the Originator runs only through the First Intellect, and there is no other road. There is no intimate discourse with Allah, that close and private speech, except from his presence. And Allah is not declared One except through his means: the true Tawhid cannot be performed except through him. Until the First Intellect is acknowledged — until the wali (وَلِيّ), the friend and guardian set there, is acknowledged — the second perfection cannot be reached, the means cannot be sought, the discourse cannot be held, There is no god but God cannot rightly be said. A sealed letter does not leap from sender to recipient; it passes through the appointed hand, and only that hand delivers it. By this one exclusive mediation the First Intellect became the Greatest Name of Allah, His ism al-azam, and his station became the most noble and most honorable of stations.

That is the one who succeeded. Against him stands the one who failed at the same threshold, and the contrast carries the lesson. There was a second emanation — the munbaith al-thani — and he was undone not by ignorance but by a single corrupt thought. He did acknowledge the First Intellect; he conceded that the First Intellect was superior, and he recognized that both their existences were real. So far he was right. But then the wrong notion took him — the notion of equality, wahm-e masawat. He imagined that his own vision was equal to the vision of the First Intellect, the first emanation. And on that delusion he was wrecked: because of it he could not reach the second perfection.

The two perfections stand apart, and the whole error lives in the gap between them. In the first perfection, all are equal — that is what the previous gate established, equality as a matter of justice. But in the second perfection, no one is equal. None is equal to another there; each is singular, and the ranks are fixed in their order of before and after, like load-bearing walls that decide every other line in the building and cannot be moved without the building changing. The second emanation's mistake was to carry the equality that belonged to the first perfection up into the second, and to claim for his own vision a parity with the First Intellect's that the second perfection does not allow. He admitted the First Intellect's superiority and in the same breath claimed to be the equal of the first emanation — and in that contradiction he lost the second perfection altogether. To acknowledge the rank is necessary. To imagine oneself its equal is the exact error that bars the door upward. The gate stays open only for the one who passes through it as a lesser thing.

The letter closes this section at the highest point it has reached: the circle of oneness. The First Intellect is the first originated being — but the circle of the first Originator stands above him and apart, and no one has reached it, and no one can. It is the circle of oneness, dairat al-wahdat, and it admits no entry. The First Intellect is the possessor of the veil; without his means, it cannot so much as be approached. And the question was put to Sayyidna Sadiq — how can "oneness" be spoken of as a "circle" at all? He answered that "oneness" here is a special honorific, a term of particular honor, and that sanctity, quds, is likewise called a circle — a circle that the First Intellect has encompassed.

Then the letter retraces, one last time, the steps by which the First Intellect rose. First his state was the state of the first perfection. Then he looked with his essence at his essence, and took as his means the greatness of God, the Exalted — and so on, each thing following the last, each with its before and its after, yet the whole of it unfolding inside the circle of oneness into which no other being ever entered. This is the singularity of every circle: that each must be held within its own measure. And yet the matter is not in time. There is only before and after, the priority and the posteriority, qabliyyat and badiyyat, that come before time and are not the same as time. For time itself comes only from the sun, and there, in the abode of origination, there is no sun and no time — only this priority and posteriority that run ahead of time and give it its order. And the Word, There is no god but God, is the essence of the whole of it: appointed so that after seven it is broken, the pen halting at the seventh letter — for it is not a circle of time at all, and there even a single point is its own circle, complete in itself, needing nothing outside it to be whole.

Here the account closes, in the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. The form looked, and knew, and emptied himself, and was given the Word; he became veil and gate and Greatest Name, while another, at the same threshold, mistook the rank for a thing he could stand level with, and fell back. What this leaves standing is the second perfection itself — the perfection no one enters as an equal, the one that the gate of the First Intellect alone opens onto. The door has been appointed; one has passed through it, and one has been turned away at it. What lies on the other side is what now must be learned.
